synopsis: Did a presbytery violate the BCO or clearly err by dissolving a congregation without its consent? The SJC said no and denied the complaint. On the constitutional issue, it held that BCO 13-9.f grants dissolution power and BCO 40-6 does not impose formal process for it. On the discretionary issue, it found no clear error in the record. The denial left dissolution in place and warned that such action still requires sufficient justification and prudent, reviewable procedure.

synopsis: The SJC sustained Psiaki’s complaint and held that the CPC Session erred by ordaining and installing officers elected at a February 5, 2023 congregational meeting where the congregation’s bylaw excluded communing members under 18 from voting. Reading BCO 6-4, 25-1, and 25-7 together, the SJC ruled that all communing members are entitled to vote and that local bylaws cannot impose an age restriction; the “good and regular standing” language addresses censure, not age. The decision did not annul the completed ordination/installation, but required future elections and installations to comply with the Constitution.

title: Jones v. Louisiana
synopsis: Louisiana Presbytery’s refusal to institute process after examining Steve Wilkins’s Federal Vision teachings was challenged for applying the wrong constitutional standard and overlooking a strong presumption that some views were out of conformity with the Westminster Standards. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled Presbytery’s denial. A “difference” need not expressly contradict the Standards; Presbytery must independently investigate and classify it rather than accept the member’s assurance or shift the burden to objectors. The ruling did not adjudicate Wilkins’s guilt; the Central Carolina memorial remained before the SJC.

synopsis: Malone challenged Presbytery’s approval of a commission’s judgment and indefinite suspension imposed without process. The SJC sustained the complaint in part and vacated the judgment and censure: the commission had authority only to investigate, and Malone’s general acknowledgments neither confessed specific charges nor showed intent to waive process under BCO 38-1. Presbytery could begin anew under proper procedures. The SJC rejected Malone’s claim that suggested steps evidencing repentance improperly bound him, treating them as noncompulsory pastoral advice.

synopsis: Marusich challenged Presbytery’s receipt of a commission’s finding that accusations against a teaching elder did not establish a strong presumption of guilt, and the commission’s failure to provide minutes or a full report. Without answering either issue or identifying an error, the SJC remanded for a new BCO 31-2 investigation, a narrative of the evidence, and a recommendation for Presbytery’s consideration under regular orders. The decision expressly establishes no general rule for BCO 31-2 investigations.

title: Choon Soon Lee v. Korean Capital Presbytery
synopsis: Korean Capital Presbytery approved a three-year suspension from the sacraments after its special judicial commission found RE Choon Soon Lee guilty of contumacy and making a false statement on a civil-court document. On appeal, the SJC sustained and reversed. Because Lee was a communicant member, the Session—not Presbytery or its commission—was the court of original jurisdiction; the commission's adjudication therefore violated constitutional standards. The SJC did not decide the underlying charges, and one commissioner dissented.

title: Sang Soo Ryoo v. Korean Capital Presbytery
snippet: 9. Under these circumstances, TE Ryoo participated in efforts to call a special meeting of KCP. When no meeting was scheduled, TE Ryoo participated in the callof a meeting in accordance with BCO 13-12.

occurrences.excerpt: 9. Under these circumstances, TE Ryoo participated in efforts to call a special meeting of KCP. When no meeting was scheduled, TE Ryoo participated in the callof a meeting in accordance with BCO 13-12.

synopsis: The SJC sustained an assistant pastor’s appeal from a three-year suspension from the sacraments after a Korean Capital Presbytery commission found him guilty of participating in the call of an allegedly unconstitutional presbytery meeting. The decisive defect was procedural: no indictment was served, no prosecutor was clearly appointed, and no trial minutes appeared in the record; service of an indictment with a witness list was critical. The case was remanded for a new trial, and the SJC expressly did not reach the merits or citation adequacy.

title: Sung Keon Kim v. Korean Capital Presbytery
snippet: 7. Under these circumstances, TE Kim participated in efforts to call a special meeting of KCP. When no meeting was scheduled, TE Kim participated in the call of a meeting in accordance with BCO 13-12.

occurrences.excerpt: 7. Under these circumstances, TE Kim participated in efforts to call a special meeting of KCP. When no meeting was scheduled, TE Kim participated in the call of a meeting in accordance with BCO 13-12.

synopsis: On appeal from a minister’s deposition in a conflicted Korean Capital Presbytery church, the SJC asked whether the commission followed BCO procedures in instituting and conducting judicial process. It sustained the appeal, holding that no indictment appears to have been served and the record lacked minutes showing a trial, contrary to BCO 32-3’s writing, indictment, and service requirements. The SJC remanded to Presbytery for a new trial under BCO 32 and 34. It expressly did not rule on the adequacy of the citations or the merits.

title: Brian Abshire v. Pacific Northwest Presbytery
snippet: It is noted that BCO 13-12 states that the purpose of the called meeting shall be stated in the notice and that "no other business other than that named in the notice is to be transacted."

occurrences.excerpt: It is noted that BCO 13-12 states that the purpose of the called meeting shall be stated in the notice and that "no other business other than that named in the notice is to be transacted."

synopsis: Abshire challenged Presbytery’s commission for its appointment, scope, exhortation, summary disposition of two elders’ complaint, and other actions. The SJC sustained only the challenge to deciding the elders’ complaint without BCO 43 procedures and remanded that complaint. It denied the other issues: the commission could conduct the required investigation, the scope objection was untimely, and its exhortation and report were pastoral rather than formal discipline. A separate sixth issue remained before Presbytery and was not decided.

synopsis: The SJC denied TE Stuart H. Merriam's appeal from Tennessee Valley Presbytery's April 20, 2002 conviction on three ordination-vow specifications and its indefinite suspension. It rejected procedural challenges—that the earlier called meeting was improperly convened and that TVP was prejudiced by prior cases—and found no clear error, applying BCO 39-3(2)'s deference to lower-court factual findings. The SJC sustained TVP's judgment; prior SJC Cases 95-10 and 96-7 had only indirect bearing and did not require retrial.

synopsis: The SJC sustained a session's timely complaint that Louisiana Presbytery barred one of its members from the Lord's Table after assuming original jurisdiction. Under BCO 33-1, a presbytery may assume jurisdiction only when the session 'refuses to act'; because the session had investigated and found no strong presumption of guilt, it acted, so LAP never acquired jurisdiction. The censure was therefore a nullity, and the member remained under his session. The SJC also held the jurisdictional assumption reviewable despite no timely complaint against it. Three commissioners dissented.

synopsis: The SJC sustained Psiaki’s complaint and held that the CPC Session erred by ordaining and installing officers elected at a February 5, 2023 congregational meeting where the congregation’s bylaw excluded communing members under 18 from voting. Reading BCO 6-4, 25-1, and 25-7 together, the SJC ruled that all communing members are entitled to vote and that local bylaws cannot impose an age restriction; the “good and regular standing” language addresses censure, not age. The decision did not annul the completed ordination/installation, but required future elections and installations to comply with the Constitution.

synopsis: The SJC sustained TE Craig Sheppard's complaint against Highlands Presbytery. It held that Presbytery erred when its Judicial Commission found a strong presumption of guilt but, instead of instituting process under BCO 31-2, directed pastoral reconciliation and conditioned later process on its success; that motion also impaired the accused's right against self-incrimination. It further held that BCO 32-20's one-year time bar had run and that the 2022 amendment did not apply retroactively, so Presbytery is debarred from prosecuting the allegations. Four commissioners dissented, disputing the BCO 32-20 ruling.

synopsis: Pacific Northwest Presbytery adopted a report finding TE Peter Leithart's views not out of accord with the fundamentals of the system of doctrine. The SJC sustained a complaint, holding PNW erred because, without formal judicial process, it lacked authority to declare either that the views were out of accord or that they were not. synopsis: Louisiana Presbytery’s refusal to institute process after examining Steve Wilkins’s Federal Vision teachings was challenged for applying the wrong constitutional standard and overlooking a strong presumption that some views were out of conformity with the Westminster Standards. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled Presbytery’s denial. A “difference” need not expressly contradict the Standards; Presbytery must independently investigate and classify it rather than accept the member’s assurance or shift the burden to objectors. The ruling did not adjudicate Wilkins’s guilt; the Central Carolina memorial remained before the SJC.

synopsis: In a BCO 40-5 memorial, Central Carolina Presbytery alleged that Louisiana Presbytery had exonerated TE J. Steven Wilkins despite his published views on election, the church, perseverance, assurance, and baptism allegedly contradicting the Westminster Standards. The SJC sustained the memorial’s gravity and found Presbytery failed to show due diligence, ordering a recorded examination, formal responses, and report. Presbytery later met the procedural directives, but the SJC relied on Case 2007-8’s substantive finding, cited Presbytery under BCO 40-5, and appointed a prosecutor for Case 2007-14.

title: Brown v. Northern California Presbytery
synopsis: Joined with Case 2009-25; the Session of Grace Presbyterian Church complained that views 3, 4, 5, and 6 in Northern California Presbytery's resolution on diaconal practice violated the BCO. The SJC sustained the complaint on the same grounds as 2009-25, annulling the abstract resolution while declining to rule on the constitutional merits of any specific diaconal view.

title: Aven v. Ohio Valley Presbytery
topics: fundamentals of the system of doctrine
synopsis: An SJC complaint alleged that Ohio Valley Presbytery failed to comply with the SJC's prior remand in Case 2014-01, which required it to 'hear further' from TE Charles Hickey about his changed view on Larger Catechism 177. The SJC denied the complaint. It held that the prior decision neither sustained nor denied the original complaint and prescribed no particular examination procedure; Hickey's nine pages of additional affirmations, exegesis, and answers constituted hearing further, and he addressed the five identified areas at least in part. A concurrence believed the SJC could also have adjudicated the confessional-difference merits; a dissent would have found noncompliance and reached the merits.

title: Barnes v. Heartland Presbytery
topics: fundamentals of the system of doctrine
synopsis: Heartland Presbytery granted a transferring OPC teaching elder an exception to WCF 19, judging his stated differences 'more than semantic but not out of accord with any fundamental.' The SJC sustained a complaint not against the merits of that judgment but against the sufficiency of the record supporting it. It held Presbytery clearly erred by failing to develop a sufficient record: the presbyters as a whole did not receive OPCUS's adverse actions, its teaching restriction, or the elder's longer paper. Remanded for those materials and release documentation to be included in the minutes. A concurrence addressed deference; four dissenters found no clear error.

synopsis: After her session erased her from the roll, Anna Lewis filed a BCO 40-5 report directly with the SJC, alleging the Presbytery of the Mississippi Valley failed to redress the session's alleged failure to give BCO 38-4 notice. The SJC held the filing out of order: under RAO 16-10.c and OMSJC Chapter 15, BCO Chapter 40 matters come to it only by General Assembly referral. It did not decide the merits, but noted that without proper notice Lewis remains a member unless she joined another church. Dissents disputed that limitation and cited past direct reviews.

synopsis: A BCO 40-5 citation arose from Metro New York Presbytery's failure to redress a session that allowed a woman to expound Scripture in place of the sermon preceding the Lord's Supper, held services without preaching, and celebrated the Supper without a preceding sermon. The SJC remitted the matter to the presbytery for constitutional resolution because the session's later no-exception response was clearly inadequate and the unapproved minutes were unclear. Presbytery must complete its work with TE Higgins and Trinity Presbyterian Church's session and report to the 51st General Assembly. A separate procedural note questioned the Assembly's direct referral but did not void it.

title: BCO 40-5 Matter re NW Georgia
synopsis: Presbytery approved calls and installed three associate pastors after a constitutionally deficient election. The SJC found egregious error, including slate voting, a standing rather than ballot vote, and failure to determine and record the number of voters present under the then-current rule. It nevertheless denied the requested annulment of the installations because PCA judicial proceedings supplied no precedent and the remedy's legitimacy was doubtful. The SJC stayed further proceedings and declared the report concluded.

synopsis: Biese and others complained that Tennessee Valley Presbytery erred by approving Redeemer Church session minutes without exception—minutes noting a youth Super Bowl party—and by denying their complaint seeking a Sabbath exception. A concurrence said the denial did not decide the Sabbath merits; a dissent would have held the complaint judicially out of order for lack of SJC jurisdiction over presbytery record review.

synopsis: The SJC denied Hopper's complaint against James River Presbytery's April 13, 1991 order barring him from teaching or preaching his views on prophecy and tongues. It rejected all five specifications: Scripture did not forbid the order; the 1974 Pastoral Letter did not address presbytery's power to enjoin such teaching; forbearance did not preclude protecting peace and purity; presbytery could restrict preaching short of a heresy finding without binding conscience; and allowing presbyteral discussion while restricting congregational teaching was not inconsistent. The action remained in force.

synopsis: Black challenged Presbytery’s handling of his complaint and its ruling that a licentiate’s non-24-hour creation-day view was not an exception to the Westminster Standards. The SJC denied remand because Presbytery had effectively adjudicated the complaint; the separate objection to proceeding without Black was not first filed below and was administratively out of order. It upheld Presbytery’s ruling that not every non-Calendar-Day view constitutes an exception. Because the record did not identify the licentiate’s precise view, the decision did not determine its acceptability or whether it could be taught.

synopsis: A member challenged Presbytery’s affirmance of his excommunication, contending that SJC Case 97-9 had reversed his four guilty verdicts and precluded increased censure. The SJC did not sustain either issue. Case 97-9 had reversed only the original censure, leaving guilt intact. Because the offender bore the burden of showing repentance, and Session’s contrary factual determination received great deference absent clear error, the later excommunication remained in effect.

synopsis: After Korean Capital Presbytery appointed a commission to suspend the functions of Korean Presbyterian Church Washington’s elected Session and replace them without prior congregational consent, TE Sung Keon Kim complained. The SJC sustained the complaint, holding that Presbytery violated Preliminary Principle Six and BCO 16-2, misread BCO 13-9, and impermissibly sought to act for the lower court. title: Dailey v. Heritage Presbytery
synopsis: Heritage Presbytery treated a member's September 2016 filing against her session as a BCO 43-3 complaint and began adjudicating it. The session timely ruled the filing did not meet BCO 43-1 and did consider it, so neither condition applied. Presbytery's post-November 12, 2016 adjudicative actions were annulled; possible underlying disciplinary matters were left to BCO 31-2 and 40-5.

It further held that BCO 32-20's one-year time bar had run and that the 2022 amendment did not apply retroactively, so Presbytery is debarred from prosecuting the allegations. Four commissioners dissented, disputing the BCO 32-20 ruling.

The ruling did not restrict Presbytery’s ability to adopt general position statements outside an investigation.

synopsis: A teaching elder appealed his judgment and deposition for refusing Presbytery committee directives and allegedly avoiding accountability. The SJC sustained five of nine specifications, holding that the committee could not impose requirements lacking constitutional warrant or control an independent mission board; vague allegations and testimony unavailable for cross-examination also impaired the trial. Because the record did not prove an ongoing pattern of insubordination, it vacated the censure and remanded for a constitutionally compliant proceeding or dismissal. Three specifications failed, while one duplicated another.

title: Dailey v. Heritage Presbytery
synopsis: Heritage Presbytery treated a member's September 2016 filing against her session as a BCO 43-3 complaint and began adjudicating it. The SJC sustained RE Scott Dailey's complaint against that action. BCO 43-3 allows higher-court review only if the lower court denies a complaint or fails to consider it by its next stated meeting. The session timely ruled the filing did not meet BCO 43-1 and did consider it, so neither condition applied. Presbytery's post-November 12, 2016 adjudicative actions were annulled; possible underlying disciplinary matters were left to BCO 31-2 and 40-5.

The Commission held a committee recommendation is not judicial action, no special instruction was required, the BCO 31-2 steps were followed, and the wording did not violate the accused’s rights.

synopsis: A ruling elder challenged Session’s elder-term proposal and its creation of Judicial and Governance Commissions. The SJC denied the first two claims: the Constitution does not regulate elder terms, and the Judicial Commission’s assigned business was sufficiently defined. It sustained the Governance Commission claim because sweeping authority and reversed delegation allowed that body to function as Session itself, contrary to BCO 15-1. Session’s third motion was annulled, but Session remained free to adopt a narrower, constitutionally compliant plan.

title: Speck v. Missouri Presbytery
synopsis: Speck challenged Missouri Presbytery’s approval of six theological judgments concerning teachings at Revoice 18, its rejection of his procedural point of order, and its refusal to debate gay-couple adoption. The SJC sustained only the first issue, particularly as to Judgments 2, 3, and 5: Presbytery improperly imported BCO 34-5’s ministerial-process standard into court review and then inadequately addressed identified errors affecting church peace and purity. It rejected the procedural and adoption claims and remanded for a focused new hearing under BCO 11-3, 11-4, and 13-9(f).

synopsis: A BCO 40-5 citation arose from Metro New York Presbytery's failure to redress a session that allowed a woman to expound Scripture in place of the sermon preceding the Lord's Supper, held services without preaching, and celebrated the Supper without a preceding sermon. The SJC remitted the matter to the presbytery for constitutional resolution because the session's later no-exception response was clearly inadequate and the unapproved minutes were unclear. Presbytery must complete its work with TE Higgins and Trinity Presbyterian Church's session and report to the 51st General Assembly. A separate procedural note questioned the Assembly's direct referral but did not void it.

title: BCO 40-5 Matter re NW Georgia
synopsis: Presbytery approved calls and installed three associate pastors after a constitutionally deficient election. The SJC found egregious error, including slate voting, a standing rather than ballot vote, and failure to determine and record the number of voters present under the then-current rule. It nevertheless denied the requested annulment of the installations because PCA judicial proceedings supplied no precedent and the remedy's legitimacy was doubtful. The SJC stayed further proceedings and declared the report concluded.

It annulled the classification and remanded for clarification and a new judgment, without deciding whether the clarified view would be acceptable.

synopsis: Teaching Elder Wallace Marshall complained against the same Eastern Carolina Presbytery actions at Fuller Memorial Presbyterian Church that were the subject of Case 90-4, filed separately as a Teaching Elder complainant. The SJC sustained this complaint on essentially the same grounds as Case 90-4, finding that the presbytery lacked authority to suspend the session without due process and to constitute itself as a 'Session Pro Tem.'

synopsis: After a church member and deacon was excommunicated by his session, he appealed to Evangel Presbytery. Presbytery found the appeal in order and appointed a commission, but then rescinded that action and never adjudicated the appeal. The SJC held Presbytery erred by failing to notify the appellant of the appeal hearing and by failing to adjudicate an appeal properly before it. It remanded under BCO 42-9 for proper adjudication and made no ruling on the remaining session-related merits issues.

title: Nickoley v. Rocky Mountain
synopsis: Rocky Mountain Presbytery cited Pastor Bruce Nickoley for contumacy during his trial, after he allegedly refused to tell his congregation to stop picketing, and immediately deposed him without a hearing. On appeal, the SJC sustained the appeal, holding the Presbytery misapplied BCO provisions on confession, citation, refusal to testify, and deposition; Nickoley neither confessed nor refused to appear. Although presbyteries have general authority to maintain order, serious charges require due process. The SJC remanded, recommending either a new process beginning with BCO §32-3 or revocation of the deposition and reinstatement.

synopsis: The SJC sustained TE Eliot Lee's complaint against KEP for filing a civil lawsuit in New Jersey state court to adjudicate ecclesiastical matters (i.e., who was the rightful pastor of HKPC). The opinion affirms that PCA church courts have no authority to use civil courts to enforce ecclesiastical decisions, and that the PCA is a non-hierarchical denomination whose authority is moral and spiritual, not civil or coercive.

title: Payne v. Western Carolina Presbytery
synopsis: Robert Woodward, along with James Linton and Kirk Lyons, filed complaints against Western Carolina Presbytery alleging it erred when it did not find a strong presumption of guilt against TE Craig Bulkeley and when it failed to properly investigate grievances due to procedural failures and alleged denial of due process to the accusers. The cases were combined with Case 2009-5 (TE Martin Payne complaint) due to similar circumstances.

synopsis: After Korean Eastern Presbytery tried, convicted, deposed, and excommunicated TE Eliot Lee, the SJC sustained his appeal and reversed the disposition and excommunication. The decisive reason was procedural: the record did not show timely service of the indictment/citations or the required 14-day trial notice, violating BCO 32-3, 32-7, and 32-10. Under BCO 42-9, the SJC rendered the decision it thought should have been made, finding no strong presumption of guilt under BCO 31-2 justified formal process; it added pastoral counsel, expressly not censure.

title: Dunn v. Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC held TE Dwight Dunn's complaint administratively out of order under OMSJC 9.1 and directed Presbytery to remedy the deficiencies by its next Stated Meeting before further action under OMSJC 9.2. The original complaint had been transmitted to the Faith Church Commission by the Stated Clerk, not committed by Presbytery motion as BCO 15-3 requires, and after the Commission denied it, the Commission did not seek Presbytery approval of its judgment. Because Presbytery had not acted, the SJC complaint was premature; no merits were reached.

synopsis: The complaint challenged Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery’s November 17, 2012 vote adopting its Complaint Commission’s recommendation to institute process and try TE David Swavely. The SJC did not sustain it. Although the record showed possible procedural irregularities—including unauthorized circulation of an earlier complaint—the SJC found no reversible error: presbyteries receive deference on factual records and broad latitude to judge the sufficiency of investigations. The recommendation to proceed to trial stands, subject to later parliamentary action. The SJC did not decide Swavely’s guilt.

title: Harwell et al. v. Nashville Presbytery
synopsis: Complainants sought review of Nashville Presbytery's August 9, 2016 actions but filed directly with the SJC instead of first with Presbytery. The SJC held the complaint judicially out of order and unable to be put in order: the initial filing was not a complaint against an act or decision (BCO 43-1) but suggested charges or an investigation request (BCO 31-2); BCO 43-2 required prior filing with Presbytery, and the sixty-day period had run. The complaint was dismissed without a merits ruling.

synopsis: Did a presbytery violate the BCO or clearly err by dissolving a congregation without its consent? The SJC said no and denied the complaint. On the constitutional issue, it held that BCO 13-9.f grants dissolution power and BCO 40-6 does not impose formal process for it. On the discretionary issue, it found no clear error in the record. The denial left dissolution in place and warned that such action still requires sufficient justification and prudent, reviewable procedure.

synopsis: Malone challenged Presbytery’s approval of a commission’s judgment and indefinite suspension imposed without process. The SJC sustained the complaint in part and vacated the judgment and censure: the commission had authority only to investigate, and Malone’s general acknowledgments neither confessed specific charges nor showed intent to waive process under BCO 38-1. Presbytery could begin anew under proper procedures. The SJC rejected Malone’s claim that suggested steps evidencing repentance improperly bound him, treating them as noncompulsory pastoral advice.

synopsis: A ruling elder challenged Session’s elder-term proposal and its creation of Judicial and Governance Commissions. The SJC denied the first two claims: the Constitution does not regulate elder terms, and the Judicial Commission’s assigned business was sufficiently defined. It sustained the Governance Commission claim because sweeping authority and reversed delegation allowed that body to function as Session itself, contrary to BCO 15-1. Session’s third motion was annulled, but Session remained free to adopt a narrower, constitutionally compliant plan.

title: Speck v. Missouri Presbytery
synopsis: Speck challenged Missouri Presbytery’s approval of six theological judgments concerning teachings at Revoice 18, its rejection of his procedural point of order, and its refusal to debate gay-couple adoption. The SJC sustained only the first issue, particularly as to Judgments 2, 3, and 5: Presbytery improperly imported BCO 34-5’s ministerial-process standard into court review and then inadequately addressed identified errors affecting church peace and purity. It rejected the procedural and adoption claims and remanded for a focused new hearing under BCO 11-3, 11-4, and 13-9(f).

The SJC framed two issues and answered both yes: the Presbytery could constitutionally adopt its Investigative Committee report and decline judicial process, because the Committee found no “strong presumption of guilt” under BCO 31-2; and it could refuse voluntary-prosecutor status, because BCO 31-1/31-3 left discipline to the Presbytery and made any voluntary prosecutor subject to its approval. The complaint was denied on both issues.

title: Parks et al. v. Central Carolina Presbytery
synopsis: Complainants challenged a Session plan under which most elders voluntarily resigned, the Session granted severance and benefits to its former pastor, proposed about a year with an interim pastor before a permanent call, and contemplated revising local bylaws. The SJC denied all four items. It held that the BCO permitted jointly considered voluntary resignations, that severance concerned resignation and the budget rather than a pastoral call, and that the plan and bylaw proposal were not themselves unconstitutional. Any later call still had to follow the BCO without undue delay, and local bylaws had to remain consistent with it.

title: Fitzsimmons v. Evangel Presbytery
synopsis: After a church member and deacon was excommunicated by his session, he appealed to Evangel Presbytery. Presbytery found the appeal in order and appointed a commission, but then rescinded that action and never adjudicated the appeal. The SJC held Presbytery erred by failing to notify the appellant of the appeal hearing and by failing to adjudicate an appeal properly before it. It remanded under BCO 42-9 for proper adjudication and made no ruling on the remaining session-related merits issues.

title: Nickoley v. Rocky Mountain
synopsis: Rocky Mountain Presbytery cited Pastor Bruce Nickoley for contumacy during his trial, after he allegedly refused to tell his congregation to stop picketing, and immediately deposed him without a hearing. On appeal, the SJC sustained the appeal, holding the Presbytery misapplied BCO provisions on confession, citation, refusal to testify, and deposition; Nickoley neither confessed nor refused to appear. Although presbyteries have general authority to maintain order, serious charges require due process. The SJC remanded, recommending either a new process beginning with BCO §32-3 or revocation of the deposition and reinstatement.

synopsis: The St. Paul Session and other Central Florida presbyters complained that Presbytery wrongly sustained a commission report denying the Session complaint and declining to find a strong presumption of guilt against Pastor John Hutchinson. The SJC denied the complaint on both issues. It held CFP permissibly directed a BCO 31-2 investigation and chose its own procedures; procedural irregularities and possible bias did not show BCO 39-3 clear error, though the panel criticized CFP’s handling. A lone dissent would remand, alleging the commission ignored the substance of 41 of 45 specifications.

The full SJC approved that action on October 16, 2003. No merits ruling or later dismissal is stated; the Manual only outlines a possible dismissal route.

synopsis: A church session suspended a member from the Lord's Table and found her guilty of contumacy. The chairman of Presbytery's Judicial Business Committee advised her that her appeal was out of order; Presbytery later ruled her complaint untimely. The SJC sustained her complaint: she had submitted to regular trial, making her appeal in order under BCO 42-2, and her complaint was timely after Presbytery's advice caused the appeal to be renamed. It remanded for Presbytery to adjudicate the appeal. Filing the appeal suspended the Lord's Table censure pending final adjudication; the SJC questioned the contumacy ruling.

title: Kim v. Korean Eastern Presbytery (Complaint)
synopsis: A minister challenged Presbytery’s denial of his complaints concerning a congregational petition and an Administrative Commission’s actions. The SJC sustained both issues: the petition should first have gone to the Session, and Presbytery and its Commission committed additional constitutional errors. Those errors did not excuse his refusal to obey Presbytery, however. Because he had been deposed in Case 2005-8, further action was moot; the SJC granted no remedy, vacatur, or remand.

topics: peace and purity of the church
synopsis: Members challenged Presbytery’s denial of their complaint against a Session instruction not to circulate an open letter repeating allegations against their pastor. The SJC denied the complaint, leaving the instruction in force. It held that liberty of conscience does not eliminate members’ obligation to obey lawful church injunctions. Here the members had sought the Session’s advice, Presbytery had found no strong presumption of chargeable offenses, and renewed circulation would disturb the church’s peace; under those circumstances, the Session acted within its authority.

title: Memorial of Central Carolina v. Louisiana
synopsis: In a BCO 40-5 memorial, Central Carolina Presbytery alleged that Louisiana Presbytery had exonerated TE J. Steven Wilkins despite his published views on election, the church, perseverance, assurance, and baptism allegedly contradicting the Westminster Standards. The SJC sustained the memorial’s gravity and found Presbytery failed to show due diligence, ordering a recorded examination, formal responses, and report. Presbytery later met the procedural directives, but the SJC relied on Case 2007-8’s substantive finding, cited Presbytery under BCO 40-5, and appointed a prosecutor for Case 2007-14.

synopsis: In this BCO 40-5 proceeding over Louisiana Presbytery’s investigation of TE Stephen Wilkins, the SJC dismissed Specification 1 because it could not find that the cited procedures were constitutionally required or that guilt was proved. The dismissal did not erase concerns about undocumented doctrinal findings; those failures were covered by Specification 2. On Presbytery’s guilty plea to that specification, the SJC imposed a public admonition for failing to find a strong presumption of doctrinal guilt and pursue trial. Wilkins’s and his church’s withdrawal made practical amends unavailable.

synopsis: Red Mountain Session challenged Presbytery’s ruling that it had inadequately addressed a member’s demand to declare his wife’s divorce unbiblical, and Presbytery’s resulting declaration and Matthew 18 instruction. The SJC sustained all four issues and reversed Presbytery. It held Session’s context-sensitive ruling disclosed no clear error, use of BCO 31-2 was reasonable, Presbytery violated BCO 15-3 by allowing its commission to revise a report after floor discussion, and Presbytery judged the wife without due process. The SJC expressly did not decide whether biblical divorce grounds existed.

The authority to receive the reference remained intact; requests from other Sessions alone did not satisfy BCO 33-1.

It directed Presbytery to note the mootness ruling in the minutes of the August 16, 2008 meeting.

synopsis: Smith challenged Presbytery’s reversal of a finding that an elder’s race-and-IQ views did not create a strong presumption of guilt and its immediate judgment against those views. The SJC upheld the reversal as a discretionary determination, without addressing its merits, but annulled the declaration against the views because a strong-presumption finding required judicial process. On remand, Presbytery was to commence process against the elder or rescind that finding and drop the matter. The ruling did not restrict Presbytery’s ability to adopt general position statements outside an investigation.

title: Lyons v. Western Carolina Presbytery
topics: BCO 34-2 scandalous charges on slight grounds
synopsis: Kirk Lyons filed BCO 32-2 charges against TE Craig Bulkeley with Western Carolina Presbytery. WCP dismissed the charges, then ruled Lyons's complaint administratively out of order for lack of standing. The SJC answered that the dismissal was not erroneous—Presbytery had discretion under BCO 31-8, 34-2, and 32-20, and the record showed no clear error—but that WCP erred on standing because Lyons's filing brought him under its jurisdiction. Because that error was not prejudicial, the SJC denied the complaint.

synopsis: An appellant under suspension from the sacraments challenged the presbytery's judicial commission process and censure. The SJC held the appeal judicially out of order—not decided on the merits—because he had not submitted to a regular trial, as BCO 42-2 requires. Treated as a complaint, it was also out of order: it had not first been presented to the presbytery, and the 30-day period had expired. The SJC further barred complaints about later court actions while he remained under censure, except as to the highest censure. The censure stood.

title: Ruff v. Nashville Presbytery
synopsis: Nashville Presbytery's BCO 31-2 investigation of reports against TE George Grant was inadequately documented and internally inconsistent, and the evidence before Presbytery raised a strong presumption of guilt, the SJC held. It sustained the complaint, ruling that pastoral reconciliation does not displace the duty to institute judicial process, and remanded for further proceedings; it did not adjudicate Grant guilty. A concurrence agreed only in remanding to supplement the record under BCO 42-5 & 7.

title: Sartorious et al. v. Siouxlands Presbytery
topics: fundamentals of the system of doctrine
synopsis: A complaint challenged Siouxlands Presbytery's investigation of allegations that TE Joshua Moon held heterodox Federal Vision views and its finding of no strong presumption of guilt. The SJC held that Presbytery had investigated diligently under BCO 31-2 and, deferring under BCO 39-3 to its credibility judgment, found no clear error. It declined to decide whether the overture should have been treated as charges because that issue was not raised below, while leaving future charges possible. A concurrence favored charges; the dissent would have found error and remanded.

synopsis: Teaching and ruling elders challenged Presbytery’s approval of TE Gregory Lawrence’s acquittal on five doctrinal charges. The SJC sustained the complaint on procedural grounds: the trial commission relied on his post-indictment exculpatory writings while he declined to testify, depriving the prosecution of cross-examination. The SJC ordered a new trial on the same indictment under specified evidentiary procedures. Because this was a complaint rather than an appeal, it did not reverse the acquittals into findings of guilt or decide the doctrinal merits.

synopsis: The SJC held TE Dwight Dunn's complaint administratively out of order under OMSJC 9.1 and directed Presbytery to remedy the deficiencies by its next Stated Meeting before further action under OMSJC 9.2. The original complaint had been transmitted to the Faith Church Commission by the Stated Clerk, not committed by Presbytery motion as BCO 15-3 requires, and after the Commission denied it, the Commission did not seek Presbytery approval of its judgment. Because Presbytery had not acted, the SJC complaint was premature; no merits were reached.

title: Dunn and Pesnell v. Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery
synopsis: The complaint challenged Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery’s November 17, 2012 vote adopting its Complaint Commission’s recommendation to institute process and try TE David Swavely. The SJC did not sustain it. Although the record showed possible procedural irregularities—including unauthorized circulation of an earlier complaint—the SJC found no reversible error: presbyteries receive deference on factual records and broad latitude to judge the sufficiency of investigations. The recommendation to proceed to trial stands, subject to later parliamentary action. The SJC did not decide Swavely’s guilt.

synopsis: A Session appealed Presbytery’s judgment finding it guilty and suspending it for refusing instructions to institute process against a member. The SJC sustained the appeal, reversed the judgment in whole, and dismissed the charges. Once Presbytery denied the member’s complaint, that matter should have ended; moreover, Presbytery did not follow BCO 40-4’s required first step before invoking BCO 40-5 review and control. The delay, prejudice, and missing-witness specifications were moot. The decision did not fault Presbytery’s underlying concern.

synopsis: A complainant challenged Nashville Presbytery's handling of allegations against a teaching elder. The SJC held the matter judicially out of order and dismissed it, finding the original filing with the church session was not a BCO 43-1 complaint because the session lacked jurisdiction over the teaching elder. Presbytery properly treated the allegations as BCO 31-2/34-1 reports, and the complainant, not a Nashville member, lacked standing to complain about that new action. A nine-member dissent argued the filing of charges conferred standing under prior SJC cases.

title: Fordice v. Pacific Northwest Presbytery
synopsis: A church member challenged Presbytery’s denial of his complaint after it resolved accusations against a minister through a BCO 38-1 confession rather than trial. The SJC held that using confession without process was not itself error, but the statement and confession failed to correlate with and address the specific allegations. It sustained the complaint, annulled the denial, and remanded for Presbytery to amend the documents, institute process, reactivate the investigative committee, or otherwise respond directly and specifically to the unresolved allegations.

synopsis: TE James Bachmann appealed Nashville Presbytery's decision to replace his judicial commission's recommended admonition with indefinite suspension. The SJC sustained the appeal: Presbytery violated BCO 15-3 by dividing the verdict and amending the censure, which it had to approve or disapprove as a whole without debate. Bachmann's earlier procedural challenges were not sustained; his unconditional post-trial confession waived them. The SJC rendered the commission's judgment and admonition as its own decision, remanded to Presbytery, and restored Bachmann to good standing, subject to possible pastoral oversight items 2–4.

synopsis: Heritage Presbytery treated a member's September 2016 filing against her session as a BCO 43-3 complaint and began adjudicating it. The SJC sustained RE Scott Dailey's complaint against that action. BCO 43-3 allows higher-court review only if the lower court denies a complaint or fails to consider it by its next stated meeting. The session timely ruled the filing did not meet BCO 43-1 and did consider it, so neither condition applied. Presbytery's post-November 12, 2016 adjudicative actions were annulled; possible underlying disciplinary matters were left to BCO 31-2 and 40-5.

title: Frazier v. Nashville Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC denied a complaint challenging Nashville Presbytery's decision not to indict a teaching elder for allegedly sinful teaching on homosexuality and same-sex attraction. The adopted judgment held that the 147-page record showed Presbytery fulfilled its BCO 31-2 investigatory duty and did not show it erred in judgment when it declined process; the complaint was denied 20-0-1. Concurring opinions raised concerns about committee recusal, record clarity, and exegetical uses of Scripture, but they were separate and did not alter the denial.

synopsis: The SJC denied a complaint challenging Heritage Presbytery’s November 12, 2016 action charging a teaching elder with violating ordination vows 6 and 7 and appointing a prosecutor to investigate and, if necessary, indict. The complaint alleged the investigating committee lacked authority for judicial process, no written report existed, and the procedure and wording violated BCO 31-2. The Commission held a committee recommendation is not judicial action, no special instruction was required, the BCO 31-2 steps were followed, and the wording did not violate the accused’s rights.

synopsis: Did a presbytery fail in its duty to condemn erroneous opinions by acquitting a minister on theological-error charges? The SJC denied the complaint, leaving the acquittal undisturbed. A complaint against a not-guilty verdict cannot provoke a retrial at the superior court; under BCO 43 the superior court may only annul or remand, not reverse, and the complainant bore the burden to show error from the record. The record contained the defendant's testimony, including recantations or clarifications, Defense Exhibit 1, and witness testimony sufficient to refrain from contradicting the trial court. The SJC expressly did not decide the defendant's actual views. A separate concurrence elaborated deference standards but did not change the judgment.

It separately found the entire process constitutionally flawed and prejudicial. The SJC reversed the whole censure, declined Presbytery’s requested harsher sentence, and concluded the matter. A concurrence disputed the majority’s BCO 32-20 interpretation while agreeing with the result.

The record noted Presbytery dismissed the commission without the BCO 15-3 vote to approve its report, but the adopted reasoning gave no further explanation and did not address that fact.

synopsis: Malone challenged Presbytery’s approval of a commission’s judgment and indefinite suspension imposed without process. The SJC sustained the complaint in part and vacated the judgment and censure: the commission had authority only to investigate, and Malone’s general acknowledgments neither confessed specific charges nor showed intent to waive process under BCO 38-1. Presbytery could begin anew under proper procedures. The SJC rejected Malone’s claim that suggested steps evidencing repentance improperly bound him, treating them as noncompulsory pastoral advice.

title: Marusich v. Central Indiana Presbytery
synopsis: Marusich challenged Presbytery’s receipt of a commission’s finding that accusations against a teaching elder did not establish a strong presumption of guilt, and the commission’s failure to provide minutes or a full report. Without answering either issue or identifying an error, the SJC remanded for a new BCO 31-2 investigation, a narrative of the evidence, and a recommendation for Presbytery’s consideration under regular orders. The decision expressly establishes no general rule for BCO 31-2 investigations.

title: Williams v. Chesapeake Presbytery
topics: case of process vs case without process
synopsis: An indicted teaching elder challenged Chesapeake Presbytery’s approval of a PJC judgment and indefinite suspension after the PJC blended a BCO 32 case of process with a BCO 38-1 case without process. The SJC sustained the complaint, annulled Presbytery’s approval, and returned the matter to the PJC. Because he admitted only some indicted charges, his negotiated confession could not satisfy BCO 38-1 and the conversion prejudiced his rights. The PJC may dismiss or proceed under BCO 32; the ruling does not decide whether conversion is ever permissible.

synopsis: A ruling elder challenged Session’s elder-term proposal and its creation of Judicial and Governance Commissions. The SJC denied the first two claims: the Constitution does not regulate elder terms, and the Judicial Commission’s assigned business was sufficiently defined. It sustained the Governance Commission claim because sweeping authority and reversed delegation allowed that body to function as Session itself, contrary to BCO 15-1. Session’s third motion was annulled, but Session remained free to adopt a narrower, constitutionally compliant plan.

title: Dudt v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery
topics: express vs. implied will of session
synopsis: A ruling elder appealed convictions for distributing an SJC decision contrary to Session's will and for allegedly false, divisive statements in an email opposing a pastoral-election proposal. The SJC sustained the appeal, reversed Session and Presbytery in whole, rendered not guilty, removed the indefinite suspension, and restored him to office. title: BCO 40-5 Matter re NW Georgia
synopsis: Presbytery approved calls and installed three associate pastors after a constitutionally deficient election. The SJC found egregious error, including slate voting, a standing rather than ballot vote, and failure to determine and record the number of voters present under the then-current rule. It nevertheless denied the requested annulment of the installations because PCA judicial proceedings supplied no precedent and the remedy's legitimacy was doubtful. The SJC stayed further proceedings and declared the report concluded.

synopsis: Two ruling-elder nominees challenged the Session’s refusal to approve them based on their theonomic views and perceived divisiveness. The full SJC denied the complaint, holding that the court of original jurisdiction may assess an unsettled theological position and whether it threatens the church’s peace, purity, or progress; divisiveness was therefore properly considered. The ruling did not decide the merits of theonomy itself, and it left undisturbed Presbytery’s annulment of the Session’s categorical statement that theonomy violated WCF 19.4.

synopsis: A member challenged Presbytery’s refusal, after investigation, to try four elders on favoritism charges and its ruling that her related complaint was out of order because dissolution of her church ended her PCA membership. The SJC denied the first item because BCO 31-2 permits declining process when investigation raises no strong presumption of guilt. It sustained the second: jurisdiction properly invoked while a communicant member is not lost through a later status change. No remand was expressly ordered.

synopsis: A congregation member complained that New River Presbytery erred in November 1991 by declining to accept TE Don Post Jr.'s resignation and dissolve his pastoral relation, instead appointing a commission. The SJC sustained the complaint. Under BCO 23-1, once the congregation concurred and no sufficient reasons to retain the pastor appeared, the resignation 'shall be accepted' and the relation dissolved; the Presbytery's general BCO 13-9 power did not override that specific provision. The Presbytery had already dissolved the relation on December 7, 1991; the adopted judgment ordered no remand. Three commissioners dissented.

synopsis: Smith challenged Northeast Presbytery’s ruling that his complaint was untimely and unconstitutional after it dissolved Grace Church and indefinitely postponed a proposed Braintree mission. The SJC sustained the complaint and remanded it for Presbytery adjudication. The May action first revealed Presbytery’s view that former members were outside the PCA, so the June complaint was timely. BCO 11-4 neither barred nor itself required care; responsibility arose here from the April referral to Presbytery’s missions committee. Care need not take the form of a mission, and mere dissolution alone would not create that responsibility.

synopsis: Complainants challenged Mississippi Valley Presbytery’s approval of James Blaha’s ordination examination, arguing that his views on tongues and prophecy were constitutional exceptions and precluded approval. The SJC agreed that Presbytery should have acknowledged and noted the exceptions, but upheld the examination. It found no proof that Blaha’s denial that the gifts conveyed revelation crossed prior Assembly limits and deferred to Presbytery on an unsettled issue. It expressly declined reexamination or remand; a substantial partial dissent would have set the examination aside.

synopsis: Mt. Carmel Session challenged New Jersey Presbytery's creation-days resolution, arguing that the Westminster Standards require six consecutive twenty-four-hour days. The SJC majority concluded that Presbytery could resolve the doctrinal question under BCO 11-4 and that prior Assembly actions permitted latitude on the length of the creation days. The General Assembly rejected the minority report, adopted the majority report, and denied the complaint.

title: Session of Harvestwood PCA v. New River Presbytery (Complaint)
synopsis: New River Presbytery treated Grace Covenant PCA's BCO 41 inquiry about a Sunday school teacher's acceptability as a request for advice, but then ruled he was eligible to teach. On Harvestwood's complaint, the SJC held that Presbytery lacked original jurisdiction to make that final disposition and that the record was unclear about the teacher's views. The SJC sustained the complaint and recommended that Presbytery rescind its March 15, 1997 action and clarify his views through proper BCO procedures; it declined to reach the creation and theistic-evolution merits.

synopsis: An individual appealed directly to the SJC, alleging her church effectively excommunicated her without process, failed the Matthew 18 process, and spiritually abused her by social isolation. The SJC dismissed as premature, without reaching the merits, because there was no record of a judicial decision by the church or of an appeal to Evangel Presbytery, the next higher court; it stated she could proceed only by providing such evidence. The severity of excommunication did not excuse that prerequisite. The SJC asked Presbytery to obtain the session's written response to her letter.

No merits review appears; the adopted vote was 18 concurring, 2 not qualified, and 4 absent.

synopsis: Did a presbytery violate the BCO or clearly err by dissolving a congregation without its consent? The SJC said no and denied the complaint. On the constitutional issue, it held that BCO 13-9.f grants dissolution power and BCO 40-6 does not impose formal process for it. On the discretionary issue, it found no clear error in the record. The denial left dissolution in place and warned that such action still requires sufficient justification and prudent, reviewable procedure.

synopsis: TE James Bachmann appealed Nashville Presbytery's decision to replace his judicial commission's recommended admonition with indefinite suspension. The SJC sustained the appeal: Presbytery violated BCO 15-3 by dividing the verdict and amending the censure, which it had to approve or disapprove as a whole without debate. Bachmann's earlier procedural challenges were not sustained; his unconditional post-trial confession waived them. The SJC rendered the commission's judgment and admonition as its own decision, remanded to Presbytery, and restored Bachmann to good standing, subject to possible pastoral oversight items 2–4.

synopsis: The SJC denied a complaint challenging Nashville Presbytery's decision not to indict a teaching elder for allegedly sinful teaching on homosexuality and same-sex attraction. The adopted judgment held that the 147-page record showed Presbytery fulfilled its BCO 31-2 investigatory duty and did not show it erred in judgment when it declined process; the complaint was denied 20-0-1. Concurring opinions raised concerns about committee recusal, record clarity, and exegetical uses of Scripture, but they were separate and did not alter the denial.

synopsis: After her session erased her from the roll, Anna Lewis filed a BCO 40-5 report directly with the SJC, alleging the Presbytery of the Mississippi Valley failed to redress the session's alleged failure to give BCO 38-4 notice. The SJC held the filing out of order: under RAO 16-10.c and OMSJC Chapter 15, BCO Chapter 40 matters come to it only by General Assembly referral. It did not decide the merits, but noted that without proper notice Lewis remains a member unless she joined another church. Dissents disputed that limitation and cited past direct reviews.

title: DeJong v. Session of Village Seven Presbyterian Church
synopsis: A ruling elder challenged Session’s elder-term proposal and its creation of Judicial and Governance Commissions. The SJC denied the first two claims: the Constitution does not regulate elder terms, and the Judicial Commission’s assigned business was sufficiently defined. It sustained the Governance Commission claim because sweeping authority and reversed delegation allowed that body to function as Session itself, contrary to BCO 15-1. Session’s third motion was annulled, but Session remained free to adopt a narrower, constitutionally compliant plan.

title: Speck v. Missouri Presbytery
synopsis: Speck challenged Missouri Presbytery’s approval of six theological judgments concerning teachings at Revoice 18, its rejection of his procedural point of order, and its refusal to debate gay-couple adoption. The SJC sustained only the first issue, particularly as to Judgments 2, 3, and 5: Presbytery improperly imported BCO 34-5’s ministerial-process standard into court review and then inadequately addressed identified errors affecting church peace and purity. It rejected the procedural and adoption claims and remanded for a focused new hearing under BCO 11-3, 11-4, and 13-9(f).

synopsis: Thornton challenged Westminster Presbytery’s refusal to place Memorial PCA Session’s call in his hands and its simultaneous initiation of administrative divestiture without censure. The SJC sustained both issues, reversed the divestiture decision, and remanded with directions to approve and deliver the call and set an installation date. A valid call supplied the congregational approbation whose absence BCO 34-10’s administrative remedy requires; Presbytery also could not rely on undisclosed concerns while avoiding required judicial process. The ruling found clear error, not an absence of all presbyterial review authority.

title: Dodson et al. v. Ohio Presbytery
synopsis: Grace PCA’s Session challenged Ohio Presbytery’s reversal of excommunication for two members convicted of heresy. The SJC partially sustained the complaint: prior indefinite suspension was not constitutionally required, but Presbytery properly found excommunication too severe because the trial record contained no evidence of contumacy. Presbytery nevertheless had to impose an appropriate lesser censure or remand for one, and lacked authority to mandate transfer to another church. The unappealed heresy convictions remained, but because the members had joined another church, further proceedings were moot.

synopsis: The SJC sustained an appeal by seven members of a 38-member mission church who were convicted by their temporary Session of opposing the organizing minister's expected election as pastor. Reversing the Presbytery's affirmance and the guilty verdicts underlying indefinite suspensions, the SJC held the indictments fatally lacked BCO 32-5 specificity; Presbytery used the wrong standard of review; the Session had no authority to control pastoral selection; and no Fifth or Ninth Commandment offense was proved. Challenges to witness-judges, venue, and refusal to refer were rejected.

synopsis: The SJC sustained Psiaki’s complaint and held that the CPC Session erred by ordaining and installing officers elected at a February 5, 2023 congregational meeting where the congregation’s bylaw excluded communing members under 18 from voting. Reading BCO 6-4, 25-1, and 25-7 together, the SJC ruled that all communing members are entitled to vote and that local bylaws cannot impose an age restriction; the “good and regular standing” language addresses censure, not age. The decision did not annul the completed ordination/installation, but required future elections and installations to comply with the Constitution.

topics: suspension of session without due process
synopsis: Ruling Elder Chappell complained against Eastern Carolina Presbytery's Commission, which had suspended the session of Fuller Memorial Presbyterian Church and constituted itself as a 'Session Pro Tem' without due process or congregational consent. The SJC sustained the complaint, holding that the BCO grants no authority for a presbytery to depose a session and act in its place, that suspension requires due process, and that the congregation has an inalienable right to be governed by officers it has chosen.

title: Marshall v. Eastern Carolina Presbytery
topics: suspension of session without due process
synopsis: Teaching Elder Wallace Marshall complained against the same Eastern Carolina Presbytery actions at Fuller Memorial Presbyterian Church that were the subject of Case 90-4, filed separately as a Teaching Elder complainant. The SJC sustained this complaint on essentially the same grounds as Case 90-4, finding that the presbytery lacked authority to suspend the session without due process and to constitute itself as a 'Session Pro Tem.'

title: Nickoley and Stephens v. Southwest Presbytery
synopsis: Complainants challenged Southwest Presbytery's January 1991 actions: withdrawing charges against two ruling elders, dissolving Pastor Pollock's pastoral relationship, and rescinding its suspension of Covenant PC's session. The SJC did not sustain the complaint and affirmed. It held the BCO gives no presbytery authority to suspend a session or act as a Session pro tem without formal congregational consent; BCO 31-1 left the elder charges with the session, so they were never validly before Presbytery; the dissolution challenge was moot after Pollock left the PCA, though Presbytery acted correctly on the congregation's request.

synopsis: A congregation member complained that New River Presbytery erred in November 1991 by declining to accept TE Don Post Jr.'s resignation and dissolve his pastoral relation, instead appointing a commission. The SJC sustained the complaint. Under BCO 23-1, once the congregation concurred and no sufficient reasons to retain the pastor appeared, the resignation 'shall be accepted' and the relation dissolved; the Presbytery's general BCO 13-9 power did not override that specific provision. The Presbytery had already dissolved the relation on December 7, 1991; the adopted judgment ordered no remand. Three commissioners dissented.

synopsis: A complaint challenged Presbytery’s suspension of a church Session and installation of a commission to perform Session functions without prior congregational consent. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled all subsequent commission actions as the Session insofar as the commission was improperly constituted. Presbytery could not suspend elected officers and replace them without prior consent; later recognition could not cure the defect. The SJC also rejected Presbytery’s objection that a related appeal barred the complaint because the cases presented fundamentally different issues.

synopsis: The SJC addressed whether a presbytery and its administrative/judicial commission could suspend a local session and assume original jurisdiction over charges against a ruling elder. It answered no: original jurisdiction belonged to the session, and a presbytery cannot "act for" a lower court by replacing congregationally elected elders. Preliminary Principle Six, BCO 16-2, and BCO 31-1/33-1 controlled; the commission's interpretation of BCO 13-9 conflicted with those principles. The Presbytery's and Commission's actions, including the censure approved by Presbytery, were reversed.

synopsis: The SJC sustained a complaint by two ruling elders against Korean Eastern Presbytery over a disputed congregational meeting (three commissioners dissented). The session was deadlocked and had not called a requested meeting; KEP's administrative commission called and supervised the February 18, 2001 meeting, and KEP approved that action. The SJC reversed both lower-court actions, holding that BCO 25-2 places responsibility on the session and that the presbytery's proper course was to adjudicate a complaint under BCO 43, not act for the session. It declined to rule on the meeting's legal effect.

synopsis: Thornton challenged Westminster Presbytery’s refusal to place Memorial PCA Session’s call in his hands and its simultaneous initiation of administrative divestiture without censure. The SJC sustained both issues, reversed the divestiture decision, and remanded with directions to approve and deliver the call and set an installation date. A valid call supplied the congregational approbation whose absence BCO 34-10’s administrative remedy requires; Presbytery also could not rely on undisclosed concerns while avoiding required judicial process. The ruling found clear error, not an absence of all presbyterial review authority.

synopsis: The SJC sustained an appeal by seven members of a 38-member mission church who were convicted by their temporary Session of opposing the organizing minister's expected election as pastor. Reversing the Presbytery's affirmance and the guilty verdicts underlying indefinite suspensions, the SJC held the indictments fatally lacked BCO 32-5 specificity; Presbytery used the wrong standard of review; the Session had no authority to control pastoral selection; and no Fifth or Ninth Commandment offense was proved. Challenges to witness-judges, venue, and refusal to refer were rejected.

synopsis: The SJC sustained Psiaki’s complaint and held that the CPC Session erred by ordaining and installing officers elected at a February 5, 2023 congregational meeting where the congregation’s bylaw excluded communing members under 18 from voting. title: Jones v. Louisiana
synopsis: Louisiana Presbytery’s refusal to institute process after examining Steve Wilkins’s Federal Vision teachings was challenged for applying the wrong constitutional standard and overlooking a strong presumption that some views were out of conformity with the Westminster Standards. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled Presbytery’s denial. A “difference” need not expressly contradict the Standards; Presbytery must independently investigate and classify it rather than accept the member’s assurance or shift the burden to objectors. The ruling did not adjudicate Wilkins’s guilt; the Central Carolina memorial remained before the SJC.

synopsis: North Florida Presbytery restored a minister deposed for adultery by a 19–17 vote. The SJC sustained the complaint, holding that Presbytery had not proceeded with the required caution and that a bare majority could not demonstrate BCO 34-8’s required strongly favorable general sentiment. It declined to require reordination, calling that question unsettled and treating BCO 37-5’s restoration pronouncement as sufficient pending clarification. The SJC annulled Presbytery’s actions concerning the minister and remanded for a proper probationary and review process.

title: Sherfey v. James River Presbytery
synopsis: Sherfey challenged James River Presbytery’s denial of his complaint and alleged errors in its commission’s proceedings. The SJC ruled the complaint judicially out of order with incurable defects: several grounds had not first been adjudicated by Presbytery as BCO 43-2 required, and the General Assembly filing missed BCO 43-3’s thirty-day deadline. Incorrect advice from Presbytery’s clerk did not excuse compliance. The adopted decision neither reached the merits nor ordered a remand; only a concurrence proposed returning the matter to Presbytery.

snippet: The CCB advised that under BCO 18-2 the extraordinary clause excuses only the six-month membership period, not the session endorsement, the two-month filing deadline, or the one-year internship sequence.

title: Phelps v. Pacific Presbytery
snippet: …PP declined to accept Irons as a candidate for the gospel ministry (per BCO 18-3), Irons was disqualified for the Office of Ruling Elder at NLB. This contention is incorrect. PP was not required to find Irons unqualified for the Office of Ruling Elder…

occurrences.excerpt: …PP declined to accept Irons as a candidate for the gospel ministry (per BCO 18-3), Irons was disqualified for the Office of Ruling Elder at NLB. This contention is incorrect. PP was not required to find Irons unqualified for the Office of Ruling Elder…

synopsis: Phelps complained that Pacific Presbytery erred by finding no constitutional irregularities in the New Life Burbank Session's ordination of Lee Irons as a ruling elder, despite PP's earlier refusal to receive Irons as a teaching-elder candidate. The SJC denied the complaint. Under BCO 39-3.3, the Court owed great deference to the lower court's discretionary fitness judgment; the single office of elder does not require identical eligibility processes, and the NLB Session had jurisdiction after Irons renounced OPC jurisdiction. PP's action stood; the SJC declined to decide the NAPARC issue.

title: Frazier v. Nashville Presbytery
snippet: convicted appellant from the Lord's Supper (BCO 18-4, 18-7, 19-2,

occurrences.excerpt: convicted appellant from the Lord's Supper (BCO 18-4, 18-7, 19-2,

synopsis: The SJC denied a complaint challenging Nashville Presbytery's decision not to indict a teaching elder for allegedly sinful teaching on homosexuality and same-sex attraction. The adopted judgment held that the 147-page record showed Presbytery fulfilled its BCO 31-2 investigatory duty and did not show it erred in judgment when it declined process; the complaint was denied 20-0-1. Concurring opinions raised concerns about committee recusal, record clarity, and exegetical uses of Scripture, but they were separate and did not alter the denial.

title: Frazier v. Nashville Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC denied a complaint challenging Nashville Presbytery's decision not to indict a teaching elder for allegedly sinful teaching on homosexuality and same-sex attraction. The adopted judgment held that the 147-page record showed Presbytery fulfilled its BCO 31-2 investigatory duty and did not show it erred in judgment when it declined process; the complaint was denied 20-0-1. Concurring opinions raised concerns about committee recusal, record clarity, and exegetical uses of Scripture, but they were separate and did not alter the denial.

title: Antioch Session v. Eastern Carolina Presbytery
snippet: 2. Did ECP err in allowing Mr. Peterson to serve as Stated Supply for at least six months on a regular basis without Licensure (BCO 19-1)?

occurrences.excerpt: 2. Did ECP err in allowing Mr. Peterson to serve as Stated Supply for at least six months on a regular basis without Licensure (BCO 19-1)?

…makes it clear that one should not be regular pulpit supply without Licensure (BCO 19-1 & 22-5 and 6). He does not fulfill any of the three categories from which pulpit supply is usually drawn (ministers, licentiates, or ruling elders). The BCO is clear…

synopsis: Antioch Session challenged Peterson’s licensure based on his prior divorce, creation and local-flood views, reversal of a committee recommendation, and close vote; it also challenged his regular preaching before licensure. The SJC rejected the licensure specifications because Presbytery had thoroughly examined repentance and doctrinal adherence, and no definitive PCA standard required exclusion on these facts. It sustained the pre-licensure supply issue under BCO 19-1, 22-5, and 22-6 and enjoined greater future circumspection. The licensure remained undisturbed; the ruling was expressly case-specific.

title: Troxell v. Presbytery of the Southwest
synopsis: A complaint challenged Presbytery’s institution of two charges against a teaching elder and related pretrial actions. The SJC annulled the household-management charge because process began fifteen months after the alleged offense and the record showed no recently flagrant, newly evident, or continuing offense under BCO 32-20. It also held that declaring the elder not in good standing removed rights without process, but left his properly imposed suspension effective. It rejected objections to discussion, questioning, and the timely submission charge, which could proceed without any determination of guilt.

title: BCO 40-5 Matter re Metropolitan NY
snippet: Furthermore, it is the position of Metropolitan New York Presbytery that it is permissible for unordained and unlicensed men to occasionally preach (BCO 19-1), but not a woman.

occurrences.excerpt: Furthermore, it is the position of Metropolitan New York Presbytery that it is permissible for unordained and unlicensed men to occasionally preach (BCO 19-1), but not a woman.

synopsis: A BCO 40-5 citation arose from Metro New York Presbytery's failure to redress a session that allowed a woman to expound Scripture in place of the sermon preceding the Lord's Supper, held services without preaching, and celebrated the Supper without a preceding sermon. The SJC remitted the matter to the presbytery for constitutional resolution because the session's later no-exception response was clearly inadequate and the unapproved minutes were unclear. Presbytery must complete its work with TE Higgins and Trinity Presbyterian Church's session and report to the 51st General Assembly. A separate procedural note questioned the Assembly's direct referral but did not void it.

occurrences.excerpt: …knowledge of church government as established by the Book of Church Order (BCO 19-2.b.3), the questions posed to them for licensure make no mention of the form of government at all. (BCO 19-3).

synopsis: The Session of Crossroads Community Church challenged Philadelphia Presbytery's licensing and ordination of a candidate who stated a difference concerning women and the office of deacon but agreed to follow the BCO. The SJC denied the complaint and affirmed Presbytery's judgment; a dissent argued it should have been sustained.

title: Frazier v. Nashville Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC denied a complaint challenging Nashville Presbytery's decision not to indict a teaching elder for allegedly sinful teaching on homosexuality and same-sex attraction. The adopted judgment held that the 147-page record showed Presbytery fulfilled its BCO 31-2 investigatory duty and did not show it erred in judgment when it declined process; the complaint was denied 20-0-1. Concurring opinions raised concerns about committee recusal, record clarity, and exegetical uses of Scripture, but they were separate and did not alter the denial.

title: Senters v. Savannah River Presbytery
snippet: …with conducting and acting upon the examinations. (See, e.g., BCO 13-6, BCO 19-2, and BCO 21-4.)

occurrences.excerpt: …with conducting and acting upon the examinations. (See, e.g., BCO 13-6, BCO 19-2, and BCO 21-4.)

synopsis: A minister challenged Presbytery’s procedures and its classification of a transfer candidate’s views on continuing tongues as “not a difference.” The SJC rejected the procedural objections because Presbytery could disregard its committee’s recommendation and had breached no required procedure. It nevertheless held that a difference need not overtly contradict the Standards and that the candidate’s statements implicated WCF 1.1 and 1.6. It annulled the classification and remanded for clarification and a new judgment, without deciding whether the clarified view would be acceptable.

snippet: …license from Philadelphia Presbytery. The four constitutional questions from BCO 19-3 were then affirmed by the licentiate. The moderator prayed and addressed licentiate with the words of BCO 19-4. A motion was then made "To record Mr. Ben Inman's…

occurrences.excerpt: …license from Philadelphia Presbytery. The four constitutional questions from BCO 19-3 were then affirmed by the licentiate. The moderator prayed and addressed licentiate with the words of BCO 19-4. A motion was then made "To record Mr. Ben Inman's…

synopsis: Black challenged Presbytery’s handling of his complaint and its ruling that a licentiate’s non-24-hour creation-day view was not an exception to the Westminster Standards. The SJC denied remand because Presbytery had effectively adjudicated the complaint; the separate objection to proceeding without Black was not first filed below and was administratively out of order. It upheld Presbytery’s ruling that not every non-Calendar-Day view constitutes an exception. Because the record did not identify the licentiate’s precise view, the decision did not determine its acceptability or whether it could be taught.

synopsis: Marusich challenged Presbytery’s receipt of a commission’s finding that accusations against a teaching elder did not establish a strong presumption of guilt, and the commission’s failure to provide minutes or a full report. Without answering either issue or identifying an error, the SJC remanded for a new BCO 31-2 investigation, a narrative of the evidence, and a recommendation for Presbytery’s consideration under regular orders. The decision expressly establishes no general rule for BCO 31-2 investigations.

title: Larry Edison et al. v. Southwest Florida Presbytery
snippet: BCO 19-6 makes it plain that no privilege is conferred in licensure

occurrences.excerpt: BCO 19-6 makes it plain that no privilege is conferred in licensure

synopsis: Ministers complained that Southwest Florida Presbytery improperly reexamined Bryan Gregory and reversed his examination, membership, and call after previously receiving him. The SJC upheld Presbytery’s authority to hear and sustain the earlier complaint but sustained the present complaint on the remedial actions. Sustaining a complaint did not itself undo prior acts; once Presbytery had treated Gregory as a member, his membership rights could be removed only through disciplinary due process. The SJC annulled the reexamination and March 24 actions and directed Presbytery to consider appropriate remedies. Gregory’s theology was not before it.

title: Frazier v. Nashville Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC denied a complaint challenging Nashville Presbytery's decision not to indict a teaching elder for allegedly sinful teaching on homosexuality and same-sex attraction. The adopted judgment held that the 147-page record showed Presbytery fulfilled its BCO 31-2 investigatory duty and did not show it erred in judgment when it declined process; the complaint was denied 20-0-1. Concurring opinions raised concerns about committee recusal, record clarity, and exegetical uses of Scripture, but they were separate and did not alter the denial.

synopsis: The SJC sustained Psiaki’s complaint and held that the CPC Session erred by ordaining and installing officers elected at a February 5, 2023 congregational meeting where the congregation’s bylaw excluded communing members under 18 from voting. synopsis: A church member challenged Heritage Presbytery's ruling that the BCO neither expressly nor implicitly requires a congregation to approve changes in a pastor's call, and that it does not require the session to publicize budget details. The SJC held the BCO silent on both points: once the original call and terms are approved, later changes are budgetary and belong to the session under BCO 12-5b; publicizing the budget is prudent but not mandated. The complaint was not sustained; seven commissioners dissented, arguing congregational approval follows by good and necessary consequence.
