synopsis: An appeal from a Presbytery judgment and indefinite suspension of a pastor turned on whether he violated the Ninth Commandment and ordination/installation vows by telling the congregation the Session had 'demanded' his resignation for six weeks. The SJC denied the appeal, holding the Session as a whole had not formally demanded resignation; individual elders' earlier opinions did not excuse the overstatement, which harmed the Session's good name. It also found no due-process irregularity or prejudice warranting reversal, deferring to the lower court under BCO 39-3, leaving indefinite suspension in place.

title: Smith v. Southwest Presbytery
synopsis: Smith appealed discipline for divisiveness, gossip and slander, broken membership vows, and contumacy arising largely from complaints and letters during church conflict. The SJC sustained her appeal, reversed guilt on all four charges, and annulled suspension from the sacraments. The documentary record proved none of the allegations; filing complaints was not itself divisiveness, and the trial improperly lacked a witness, shifted proof to Smith, showed prejudice, and unfairly rejected her written defense. The SJC declined remand because the evidence was insufficient.

The SJC affirmed KEP's denial and the guilt findings, but reversed the increased censures. An appellate court may not increase a censure under BCO 42-9; the trial court retains discretion to remove or increase an indefinite suspension, though the appellate court may recommend a lesser censure. The SJC sustained TVP's judgment; prior SJC Cases 95-10 and 96-7 had only indirect bearing and did not require retrial.

title: Jones v. Louisiana
synopsis: Louisiana Presbytery’s refusal to institute process after examining Steve Wilkins’s Federal Vision teachings was challenged for applying the wrong constitutional standard and overlooking a strong presumption that some views were out of conformity with the Westminster Standards. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled Presbytery’s denial. A “difference” need not expressly contradict the Standards; Presbytery must independently investigate and classify it rather than accept the member’s assurance or shift the burden to objectors. The ruling did not adjudicate Wilkins’s guilt; the Central Carolina memorial remained before the SJC.

title: White v. Siouxlands Presbytery
synopsis: A minister complained that his presbytery wrongly refused to order a BCO 31-2 investigation into another minister’s Covenant of Works/Federal Vision views. The SJC sustained the complaint and remanded for that investigation, holding that BCO 31-2 requires investigation of credible, injurious reports about Christian character. The presbytery erred by applying the higher evidentiary standard for conviction after process; reports sufficient to trigger investigation need not establish guilt or a strong presumption of guilt, and hearsay or conflicting testimony can require investigation rather than justify refusal. A concurrence agreed in result; the dissent found no clear error in the presbytery’s exercise of discretion.

title: McNeil v. Chesapeake Presbytery
synopsis: An appellant under suspension from the sacraments challenged the presbytery's judicial commission process and censure. The SJC held the appeal judicially out of order—not decided on the merits—because he had not submitted to a regular trial, as BCO 42-2 requires. Treated as a complaint, it was also out of order: it had not first been presented to the presbytery, and the 30-day period had expired. The SJC further barred complaints about later court actions while he remained under censure, except as to the highest censure. The censure stood.

synopsis: Phelps complained that Pacific Presbytery erred by finding no constitutional irregularities in the New Life Burbank Session's ordination of Lee Irons as a ruling elder, despite PP's earlier refusal to receive Irons as a teaching-elder candidate. The SJC denied the complaint. Under BCO 39-3.3, the Court owed great deference to the lower court's discretionary fitness judgment; the single office of elder does not require identical eligibility processes, and the NLB Session had jurisdiction after Irons renounced OPC jurisdiction. PP's action stood; the SJC declined to decide the NAPARC issue.

title: Ruff v. Nashville Presbytery
synopsis: Nashville Presbytery's BCO 31-2 investigation of reports against TE George Grant was inadequately documented and internally inconsistent, and the evidence before Presbytery raised a strong presumption of guilt, the SJC held. It sustained the complaint, ruling that pastoral reconciliation does not displace the duty to institute judicial process, and remanded for further proceedings; it did not adjudicate Grant guilty. A concurrence agreed only in remanding to supplement the record under BCO 42-5 & 7.

The SJC held that Presbytery had investigated diligently under BCO 31-2 and, deferring under BCO 39-3 to its credibility judgment, found no clear error. It declined to decide whether the overture should have been treated as charges because that issue was not raised below, while leaving future charges possible. A concurrence favored charges; the dissent would have found error and remanded.

title: Jennings v. North Florida Presbytery
synopsis: North Florida Presbytery restored a minister deposed for adultery by a 19–17 vote. It declined to require reordination, calling that question unsettled and treating BCO 37-5’s restoration pronouncement as sufficient pending clarification. The SJC annulled Presbytery’s actions concerning the minister and remanded for a proper probationary and review process.

synopsis: The SJC dismissed Matt Ruff's complaint against Nashville Presbytery as judicially out of order under OMSJC 10.5.a. Ruff challenged Presbytery's failure to investigate a teaching elder, but BCO 43 requires a complaint against an act or decision; lack of action qualifies only when a court meeting has occurred and the court failed to act. Presbytery's nearest antecedent meeting was August 18, 2010, and Ruff filed October 27, 2010, beyond BCO 43-2's thirty-day limit. Because the defect could not be cured, the case was dismissed without reaching the merits; a separate objection disputed that ruling.

The SJC rejected prejudice, irregularity, and venue claims, voided the trial judgment, and noted that his expired prior suspension left him a presbytery member without call. synopsis: TE John Hardie appealed his Metro Atlanta Presbytery conviction on three charges of breaking ordination vows and indefinite suspension, alleging seventeen procedural and evidentiary errors. Applying BCO 39-2/3 clear-error deference, the SJC denied every specification and upheld the judgment and censure. It found no clear error in the BCO 31-2 investigation, indictment/prosecutor process, commission membership, evidence rulings, scheduling, alleged prejudice, or censure. It assessed transcription costs equally while encouraging MAP to absorb them, and cautioned that an absent commissioner's vote might support a future challenge.

title: Wills v. Metro Atlanta Presbytery
synopsis: After Metro Atlanta Presbytery dissolved Grace North Atlanta, a complaint challenging that action was declared administratively out of order for lacking a signature. Wills then complained to the SJC. The SJC held the SJC complaint was not properly before it and was administratively out of order: under BCO 43-2, a complaint must first go to the court whose act is challenged, and Presbytery had not yet addressed that ruling. Wills could file with Presbytery within 30 days. No merits ruling on the dissolution.

title: Aven v. Ohio Valley Presbytery
topics: fundamentals of the system of doctrine
synopsis: An SJC complaint alleged that Ohio Valley Presbytery failed to comply with the SJC's prior remand in Case 2014-01, which required it to 'hear further' from TE Charles Hickey about his changed view on Larger Catechism 177. The SJC denied the complaint. It held that the prior decision neither sustained nor denied the original complaint and prescribed no particular examination procedure; Hickey's nine pages of additional affirmations, exegesis, and answers constituted hearing further, and he addressed the five identified areas at least in part. A concurrence believed the SJC could also have adjudicated the confessional-difference merits; a dissent would have found noncompliance and reached the merits.

title: Barnes v. Heartland Presbytery
topics: fundamentals of the system of doctrine
synopsis: Heartland Presbytery granted a transferring OPC teaching elder an exception to WCF 19, judging his stated differences 'more than semantic but not out of accord with any fundamental.' The SJC sustained a complaint not against the merits of that judgment but against the sufficiency of the record supporting it. It held Presbytery clearly erred by failing to develop a sufficient record: the presbyters as a whole did not receive OPCUS's adverse actions, its teaching restriction, or the elder's longer paper. Remanded for those materials and release documentation to be included in the minutes. A concurrence addressed deference; four dissenters found no clear error.

title: Fordice v. Pacific Northwest Presbytery
synopsis: A church member challenged Presbytery’s denial of his complaint after it resolved accusations against a minister through a BCO 38-1 confession rather than trial. The SJC held that using confession without process was not itself error, but the statement and confession failed to correlate with and address the specific allegations. It sustained the complaint, annulled the denial, and remanded for Presbytery to amend the documents, institute process, reactivate the investigative committee, or otherwise respond directly and specifically to the unresolved allegations.

The denial left dissolution in place and warned that such action still requires sufficient justification and prudent, reviewable procedure.

synopsis: Did a presbytery fail in its duty to condemn erroneous opinions by acquitting a minister on theological-error charges? The SJC denied the complaint, leaving the acquittal undisturbed. A complaint against a not-guilty verdict cannot provoke a retrial at the superior court; under BCO 43 the superior court may only annul or remand, not reverse, and the complainant bore the burden to show error from the record. The record contained the defendant's testimony, including recantations or clarifications, Defense Exhibit 1, and witness testimony sufficient to refrain from contradicting the trial court. The SJC expressly did not decide the defendant's actual views. A separate concurrence elaborated deference standards but did not change the judgment.

title: Crouse v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery
synopsis: A serving deacon nominated for ruling elder complained that his session removed his nomination before BCO 24-1 instruction or examination. The SJC held the session erred by adding an unwritten pre-examination 'vetting' removal and that Northwest Georgia Presbytery erred in approving it: BCO 24-1's sequence—instruction and examination before the session determines eligibility—is mandatory. The ruling reserved the session's sound discretion and the treatment of frivolous or clearly disqualified nominees. The complaint was sustained and remanded for adjudication consistent with the decision.

synopsis: A complaint challenging a session's refusal to advance an ordained deacon's nomination for re-election to the diaconate was denied by the SJC. Northwest Georgia Presbytery had adopted its judicial commission's judgment that the session did not err; applying BCO 39-3(3)'s deference to discretionary judgments, the SJC found no clear error, held formal charges were unnecessary and re-election was not guaranteed, and refused to attribute one elder's questionable retaliation rationale to the session. The majority encouraged prompt communication of reasons. A dissent would apply BCO 39-3.4 and sustain.

title: Dodson et al. v. Ohio Presbytery
synopsis: Grace PCA’s Session challenged Ohio Presbytery’s reversal of excommunication for two members convicted of heresy. The SJC partially sustained the complaint: prior indefinite suspension was not constitutionally required, but Presbytery properly found excommunication too severe because the trial record contained no evidence of contumacy. Presbytery nevertheless had to impose an appropriate lesser censure or remand for one, and lacked authority to mandate transfer to another church. The unappealed heresy convictions remained, but because the members had joined another church, further proceedings were moot.

title: Fozard v. North Texas Presbytery

The decision, adopted 20-1, expressly did not endorse the Respondents’ Preliminary Principles arguments; a concurrence disclaimed approval of the policy, and one member dissented.

synopsis: Herron and others challenged Presbytery’s decision to proceed to trial after a BCO 31-2 finding, his administrative suspension, denial of access to Presbytery records and meetings, and a public statement. The SJC sustained only the access issue: suspension from official functions did not remove his membership rights, though it did not entitle him to every investigative-committee document. Finding no clear error on the other issues, it ordered trial to proceed, temporarily stayed censure decisions, and postponed related complaints through trial and any appeal.

title: Park et al. v. Korean Central Presbytery
synopsis: Teaching elders challenged Korean Central Presbytery’s summary censure of a minister before an indictment was prepared. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled Presbytery’s action because discipline preceded particular charges and a specific confession, and because an independent church lacked authority to impose PCA censure. It declared the underlying matter moot because the alleged event was twenty-one years old and the victim would not cooperate, ending the proceeding without remand. The ruling addressed neither the allegations’ merits nor all old charges categorically.

synopsis: The SJC sustained TE Craig Sheppard's complaint against Highlands Presbytery. It held that Presbytery erred when its Judicial Commission found a strong presumption of guilt but, instead of instituting process under BCO 31-2, directed pastoral reconciliation and conditioned later process on its success; that motion also impaired the accused's right against self-incrimination. It further held that BCO 32-20's one-year time bar had run and that the 2022 amendment did not apply retroactively, so Presbytery is debarred from prosecuting the allegations. Four commissioners dissented, disputing the BCO 32-20 ruling.

synopsis: Biese and others complained that Tennessee Valley Presbytery erred by approving Redeemer Church session minutes without exception—minutes noting a youth Super Bowl party—and by denying their complaint seeking a Sabbath exception. The SJC denied the complaint: because Presbytery gave no reasons for its actions, the record was insufficient to find it erred in interpreting the Constitution. A concurrence said the denial did not decide the Sabbath merits; a dissent would have held the complaint judicially out of order for lack of SJC jurisdiction over presbytery record review.

The SJC denied the constitutional challenge because the record reasonably supported concern for the church’s peace and spiritual welfare, but sustained the challenge to Presbytery’s lack of specific direction and poor communication. The decision distinguishes prohibited mandatory visitation without cause from a reasonably justified visit, while requiring clarity about its objectives. synopsis: An elder appealed Presbytery’s elevation, without additional process, of suspensions from office and the Sacraments to deposition and excommunication. The SJC granted the appeal, reversed in whole, and remanded, restoring the prior suspensions. Elevation required a hearing on incorrigibility and contumacy—with a charge, evidence, plea, and defense—but not a full de novo trial; disagreement with the original verdict alone was insufficient. The SJC left unresolved deposition from office when excommunication is absent.

title: Reynolds v. Pee Dee Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC dismissed Mrs. Kappie Reynolds's complaint against Pee Dee Presbytery as judicially out of order. The complaint challenged a Session's reception of and action on a confession at a meeting more than six months before filing, far outside BCO 43-2's sixty-day period; the SJC held the untimeliness was not demonstrated curable. The ruling expressly reserved whether Reynolds could proceed as an injured party under BCO 31-5 and whether the Session had jurisdiction over claims outside the received confession.

synopsis: South Florida Presbytery deposed a Teaching Elder, suspended him from the sacraments, and later excommunicated him without first assigning him to a particular church under BCO 46-8. The complainant argued that omission stripped Presbytery of jurisdiction. The SJC denied the complaint: BCO 46-8 requires assignment but fixes no timeframe or mechanism; a deposed minister remains under Presbytery's jurisdiction until transfer, and BCO 37-9(a) preserves censure authority. Deferring under BCO 39-3, the SJC found no clear error in Presbytery's efforts. Two concurrences agreed in result but disputed the majority's broad reasoning and deference.

title: Hedman v. Pacific Northwest Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC denied RE Gerald Hedman's complaint against Pacific Northwest Presbytery, which had adopted five not-guilty judgments on charges that TE Peter Leithart's baptism, covenant, imputation, justification, and union-with-Christ views contradicted the Westminster Standards. Bound to the record and clear-error review, the SJC found no procedural violation and insufficient evidence that Presbytery clearly erred. It left the verdicts undisturbed, declined to endorse Leithart's views generally, and urged continued clarification of his non-standard terminology. A separate dissent would have found error and ordered a new trial or reference.

Presbytery also had to submit amended minutes and complete, or formally plan, overdue Session-record reviews for report to the 45th General Assembly.

title: Thompson v. South Florida Presbytery
synopsis: After a Session excommunicated a member without trial for contumacy, the SJC sustained his complaint and annulled the contumacy judgment, excommunication, and later Session and Presbytery actions. No mutually agreed BCO 38-1 confession existed, and declining a confession meeting was not immediately censurable objective contumacy under BCO 32-6; subjective contumacy required confession or trial. He reverted to membership under pending indictment. The SJC did not find the indictment unconstitutional, decide trial guilt, or consider the unpleaded trespass warning.

title: Dailey v. Heritage Presbytery
synopsis: Heritage Presbytery treated a member's September 2016 filing against her session as a BCO 43-3 complaint and began adjudicating it. The SJC sustained RE Scott Dailey's complaint against that action. BCO 43-3 allows higher-court review only if the lower court denies a complaint or fails to consider it by its next stated meeting. The session timely ruled the filing did not meet BCO 43-1 and did consider it, so neither condition applied. Presbytery's post-November 12, 2016 adjudicative actions were annulled; possible underlying disciplinary matters were left to BCO 31-2 and 40-5.

The SJC remitted the matter to the presbytery for constitutional resolution because the session's later no-exception response was clearly inadequate and the unapproved minutes were unclear. A separate procedural note questioned the Assembly's direct referral but did not void it.

title: BCO 40-5 Matter re NW Georgia
synopsis: Presbytery approved calls and installed three associate pastors after a constitutionally deficient election. The SJC found egregious error, including slate voting, a standing rather than ballot vote, and failure to determine and record the number of voters present under the then-current rule. It nevertheless denied the requested annulment of the installations because PCA judicial proceedings supplied no precedent and the remedy's legitimacy was doubtful. The SJC stayed further proceedings and declared the report concluded.

topics: suspension of session without due process
synopsis: Ruling Elder Chappell complained against Eastern Carolina Presbytery's Commission, which had suspended the session of Fuller Memorial Presbyterian Church and constituted itself as a 'Session Pro Tem' without due process or congregational consent. The SJC sustained the complaint, holding that the BCO grants no authority for a presbytery to depose a session and act in its place, that suspension requires due process, and that the congregation has an inalienable right to be governed by officers it has chosen.

synopsis: Teaching Elder Wallace Marshall complained against the same Eastern Carolina Presbytery actions at Fuller Memorial Presbyterian Church that were the subject of Case 90-4, filed separately as a Teaching Elder complainant. The SJC sustained this complaint on essentially the same grounds as Case 90-4, finding that the presbytery lacked authority to suspend the session without due process and to constitute itself as a 'Session Pro Tem.'

synopsis: Korean Eastern Presbytery dismissed TE Eliot Lee's charges against two teaching elders without trial, and the SJC sustained Lee's complaint that this was unconstitutional. Although a presbytery may dismiss charges under BCO 29-1, 32-20, 34-2, or 31-8, it bears the burden of documenting that basis; KEP did not. The SJC refused Lee's request that it enter the guilt verdicts the presbytery should have reached—that power exists on appeal, not complaint. It remanded for KEP to begin process under BCO 32.

synopsis: Hahn challenged Presbytery’s ruling that CTKPC Session lawfully excluded him from that congregation’s worship until a psychiatric evaluation addressed safety concerns. The SJC denied the complaint. Applying BCO 39-3.3, it found no clear error in the lower courts’ credibility and discretionary judgments, given Session’s familiarity with the people and events. It characterized the restriction as informal pastoral safety guidance, not judicial discipline: it did not bar sacraments, worship elsewhere, or transfer, and attendance could resume upon medical assurance. The conditional local restriction therefore remained undisturbed.

title: Aven v. Ohio Valley Presbytery
topics: fundamentals of the system of doctrine
synopsis: An SJC complaint alleged that Ohio Valley Presbytery failed to comply with the SJC's prior remand in Case 2014-01, which required it to 'hear further' from TE Charles Hickey about his changed view on Larger Catechism 177. The SJC denied the complaint. It held that the prior decision neither sustained nor denied the original complaint and prescribed no particular examination procedure; Hickey's nine pages of additional affirmations, exegesis, and answers constituted hearing further, and he addressed the five identified areas at least in part. A concurrence believed the SJC could also have adjudicated the confessional-difference merits; a dissent would have found noncompliance and reached the merits.

topics: fundamentals of the system of doctrine
synopsis: Heartland Presbytery granted a transferring OPC teaching elder an exception to WCF 19, judging his stated differences 'more than semantic but not out of accord with any fundamental.' The SJC sustained a complaint not against the merits of that judgment but against the sufficiency of the record supporting it. It held Presbytery clearly erred by failing to develop a sufficient record: the presbyters as a whole did not receive OPCUS's adverse actions, its teaching restriction, or the elder's longer paper. Remanded for those materials and release documentation to be included in the minutes. A concurrence addressed deference; four dissenters found no clear error.

title: Anna Lewis v. Presbytery of the Mississippi Valley
synopsis: After her session erased her from the roll, Anna Lewis filed a BCO 40-5 report directly with the SJC, alleging the Presbytery of the Mississippi Valley failed to redress the session's alleged failure to give BCO 38-4 notice. The SJC held the filing out of order: under RAO 16-10.c and OMSJC Chapter 15, BCO Chapter 40 matters come to it only by General Assembly referral. It did not decide the merits, but noted that without proper notice Lewis remains a member unless she joined another church. Dissents disputed that limitation and cited past direct reviews.

synopsis: A minister complained that his presbytery wrongly refused to order a BCO 31-2 investigation into another minister’s Covenant of Works/Federal Vision views. The SJC sustained the complaint and remanded for that investigation, holding that BCO 31-2 requires investigation of credible, injurious reports about Christian character. The presbytery erred by applying the higher evidentiary standard for conviction after process; reports sufficient to trigger investigation need not establish guilt or a strong presumption of guilt, and hearsay or conflicting testimony can require investigation rather than justify refusal. A concurrence agreed in result; the dissent found no clear error in the presbytery’s exercise of discretion.

synopsis: A Session appealed Presbytery’s judgment finding it guilty and suspending it for refusing instructions to institute process against a member. The SJC sustained the appeal, reversed the judgment in whole, and dismissed the charges. Once Presbytery denied the member’s complaint, that matter should have ended; moreover, Presbytery did not follow BCO 40-4’s required first step before invoking BCO 40-5 review and control. The delay, prejudice, and missing-witness specifications were moot. The decision did not fault Presbytery’s underlying concern.

title: the Session of Hope Community Church v. Central Carolina Presbytery
topics: session authority over time and place of worship
synopsis: Hope Community Church’s Session challenged Presbytery’s requirement that a multi-site congregation eventually particularize its second worship site. The SJC sustained the complaint, annulled the requirement, and struck it from the Presbytery Manual because BCO 12-5e specifically entrusts the time and place of worship to the Session, which Presbytery’s general church-enlargement authority could not supersede. The narrow ruling did not resolve broader concerns about multi-site churches or eliminate Presbytery’s review of a second site’s location under BCO 13-9(g).

title: William G. Mitchell v. The Presbytery of the Ascension

Because the pivotal email was absent from the record, the SJC vacated the sabbatical-related judgment and remanded for Presbytery only to consider whether a new trial was warranted. It reversed and dismissed the clerk-duty specification because the four-month delay in submitting minutes was attributable to the Session and did not justify a trial. Only the first specification remained potentially triable.

The SJC therefore vacated the censure and dissolution of the call and remanded for reconsideration of censure; Grady's separate administrative suspension remained effective.

synopsis: A minister complained that his presbytery wrongly refused to order a BCO 31-2 investigation into another minister’s Covenant of Works/Federal Vision views. The SJC sustained the complaint and remanded for that investigation, holding that BCO 31-2 requires investigation of credible, injurious reports about Christian character. The presbytery erred by applying the higher evidentiary standard for conviction after process; reports sufficient to trigger investigation need not establish guilt or a strong presumption of guilt, and hearsay or conflicting testimony can require investigation rather than justify refusal. A concurrence agreed in result; the dissent found no clear error in the presbytery’s exercise of discretion.

synopsis: The SJC dismissed a BCO 40-5 application because the matter concerned proceedings in a judicial case in which a complaint had been filed. Under BCO 40-3, such proceedings may not be handled by review and control once notice of appeal or complaint is given to the lower court. title: Thompson v. South Florida Presbytery
synopsis: After a Session excommunicated a member without trial for contumacy, the SJC sustained his complaint and annulled the contumacy judgment, excommunication, and later Session and Presbytery actions. No mutually agreed BCO 38-1 confession existed, and declining a confession meeting was not immediately censurable objective contumacy under BCO 32-6; subjective contumacy required confession or trial. He reverted to membership under pending indictment. The SJC did not find the indictment unconstitutional, decide trial guilt, or consider the unpleaded trespass warning.

title: Wills v. Metro Atlanta Presbytery
synopsis: Did a presbytery violate the BCO or clearly err by dissolving a congregation without its consent? The SJC said no and denied the complaint. On the constitutional issue, it held that BCO 13-9.f grants dissolution power and BCO 40-6 does not impose formal process for it. On the discretionary issue, it found no clear error in the record. The denial left dissolution in place and warned that such action still requires sufficient justification and prudent, reviewable procedure.

title: Speck v. Missouri Presbytery
synopsis: Ryan Speck challenged Missouri Presbytery’s BCO 31-2 investigation and its refusal to commence process against Greg Johnson on four allegations concerning same-sex attraction as sin, identity in Christ, sanctification, and fitness for office. The SJC denied the complaint in full. It found no clear procedural error and held that Johnson’s explanations and clarifications made Presbytery’s non-indictment judgments reasonable. No trial was ordered. The ruling neither adjudged Johnson guilty nor endorsed every statement or broader constitutional position concerning same-sex attraction.

title: Session of First Presbyterian Church North Port v. Presbytery of Southwest Florida
synopsis: The SJC sustained the Session's complaint against Presbytery. Presbytery had ruled a member's original complaint administratively out of order as untimely but then remanded the matter to the Session; the SJC held that once out of order, no complaint remained to remand. It also held Presbytery could not direct or instruct the Session to initiate formal process without BCO 40-5's required citation step, so those directions were null and void. The member remained under the Session's jurisdiction; the civil trespass order was not ecclesiastical discipline and did not alter membership.

synopsis: Did a presbytery violate the BCO or clearly err by dissolving a congregation without its consent? The SJC said no and denied the complaint. On the constitutional issue, it held that BCO 13-9.f grants dissolution power and BCO 40-6 does not impose formal process for it. On the discretionary issue, it found no clear error in the record. The denial left dissolution in place and warned that such action still requires sufficient justification and prudent, reviewable procedure.

synopsis: Bowen challenged Presbytery’s attempt, two years after installation, to rescind its earlier ruling and annul local officers’ elections and ordinations without trial. The SJC sustained the complaint: ordination is perpetual, deposition requires judicial process, and rescission was out of order after implementation; Presbytery likewise could not suspend a local elder without due process. The officers remained in office but doctrinally out of accord; voluntary demission or proper process was advised.

synopsis: A complaint challenged Presbytery’s suspension of a church Session and installation of a commission to perform Session functions without prior congregational consent. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled all subsequent commission actions as the Session insofar as the commission was improperly constituted. Presbytery could not suspend elected officers and replace them without prior consent; later recognition could not cure the defect. The SJC also rejected Presbytery’s objection that a related appeal barred the complaint because the cases presented fundamentally different issues.

title: Sung Keon Kim v. Korean Capital Presbytery
synopsis: After Korean Capital Presbytery appointed a commission to suspend the functions of Korean Presbyterian Church Washington’s elected Session and replace them without prior congregational consent, TE Sung Keon Kim complained. The SJC sustained the complaint, holding that Presbytery violated Preliminary Principle Six and BCO 16-2, misread BCO 13-9, and impermissibly sought to act for the lower court. Relying on Chappell, it annulled the commission’s subsequent actions as the Session.

synopsis: On Covenant Presbytery’s mixed BCO 41 reference, the SJC held that ministers Morse and Crenshaw could not resign unilaterally; joining another evangelical church invoked BCO 38-3, requiring their names erased, with notice that they were in good standing and faced no pending charges. Grace Church’s withdrawal required a congregational vote, not notice to Presbytery, so its name also was to be erased. Grace had abandoned its complaints, rendering them moot; the SJC nevertheless opined that recording a protest is insulated from complaint by BCO 45-5.

synopsis: The St. Paul Session and other Central Florida presbyters complained that Presbytery wrongly sustained a commission report denying the Session complaint and declining to find a strong presumption of guilt against Pastor John Hutchinson. The SJC denied the complaint on both issues. It held CFP permissibly directed a BCO 31-2 investigation and chose its own procedures; procedural irregularities and possible bias did not show BCO 39-3 clear error, though the panel criticized CFP’s handling. A lone dissent would remand, alleging the commission ignored the substance of 41 of 45 specifications.

synopsis: Abshire challenged Presbytery’s commission for its appointment, scope, exhortation, summary disposition of two elders’ complaint, and other actions. The SJC sustained only the challenge to deciding the elders’ complaint without BCO 43 procedures and remanded that complaint. It denied the other issues: the commission could conduct the required investigation, the scope objection was untimely, and its exhortation and report were pastoral rather than formal discipline. A separate sixth issue remained before Presbytery and was not decided.

title: Sang Bai Kim and RE Chan Soo Kim v. Korean Eastern Presbytery
synopsis: In a dispute arising from a Korean Eastern Presbytery congregational election, two ruling elders were tried, refused to plead, and were suspended from sacraments and office; KEP denied their appeal, then increased the censures to deposition and excommunication for contumacy. The SJC affirmed KEP's denial and the guilt findings, but reversed the increased censures. An appellate court may not increase a censure under BCO 42-9; the trial court retains discretion to remove or increase an indefinite suspension, though the appellate court may recommend a lesser censure. The original suspension remained.

The full SJC approved that action on October 16, 2003. No merits ruling or later dismissal is stated; the Manual only outlines a possible dismissal route.

synopsis: Ryan Speck challenged Missouri Presbytery’s BCO 31-2 investigation and its refusal to commence process against Greg Johnson on four allegations concerning same-sex attraction as sin, identity in Christ, sanctification, and fitness for office. The SJC denied the complaint in full. It found no clear procedural error and held that Johnson’s explanations and clarifications made Presbytery’s non-indictment judgments reasonable. No trial was ordered. The ruling neither adjudged Johnson guilty nor endorsed every statement or broader constitutional position concerning same-sex attraction.

title: Benyola v. Central Florida Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC declared Benyola's complaint against Central Florida Presbytery administratively out of order and incapable of being put in order, because Benyola was no longer a member of any PCA congregation and thus lacked standing. The decision was adopted 23-0 on a roll call, one absent, on the officers' recommendation. The record does not identify the underlying presbytery action or reach the complaint's merits, so the case's value is its threshold standing ruling, not any complaint determination.

topics: peace and purity of the church
synopsis: Members challenged Presbytery’s denial of their complaint against a Session instruction not to circulate an open letter repeating allegations against their pastor. The SJC denied the complaint, leaving the instruction in force. It held that liberty of conscience does not eliminate members’ obligation to obey lawful church injunctions. synopsis: A church session suspended a member from the Lord's Table and found her guilty of contumacy. The chairman of Presbytery's Judicial Business Committee advised her that her appeal was out of order; Presbytery later ruled her complaint untimely. The SJC sustained her complaint: she had submitted to regular trial, making her appeal in order under BCO 42-2, and her complaint was timely after Presbytery's advice caused the appeal to be renamed. It remanded for Presbytery to adjudicate the appeal. Filing the appeal suspended the Lord's Table censure pending final adjudication; the SJC questioned the contumacy ruling.

title: Paul W. Lee v. Korean Southwest
synopsis: A minister appealed three convictions and suspension that would automatically become indefinite absent repentance. The SJC sustained the appeal: unauthorized committee citations and admonition without process could not support guilt, and multiple trial violations were fatally prejudicial. It set aside the judgment, dismissed the citation and admonition charges, and revoked both censures. The inappropriate-language charge was not adjudicated on its merits; Presbytery could retry it on remand or dismiss it.

title: Jennings v. North Florida Presbytery
synopsis: North Florida Presbytery restored a minister deposed for adultery by a 19–17 vote. The SJC sustained the complaint, holding that Presbytery had not proceeded with the required caution and that a bare majority could not demonstrate BCO 34-8’s required strongly favorable general sentiment. It declined to require reordination, calling that question unsettled and treating BCO 37-5’s restoration pronouncement as sufficient pending clarification. The SJC annulled Presbytery’s actions concerning the minister and remanded for a proper probationary and review process.

The inappropriate-language charge was not adjudicated on its merits; Presbytery could retry it on remand or dismiss it.

A concurrence agreed only in remanding to supplement the record under BCO 42-5 & 7.

synopsis: Marshall complained that Pacific Presbytery wrongly refused to dismiss a judicial case despite alleged procedural irregularities in the indictment and process. The SJC held the complaint judicially out of order: objections arising in a judicial case were to be preserved for appeal under BCO 32-14 and 42-3, and Marshall’s pending appeal independently barred a complaint under BCO 43-1. title: Marshall v. Pacific Presbytery
synopsis: G. Rick Marshall appealed Pacific Presbytery, which failed to transmit a material part of the Record of the Case, causing irremediable injury. The SJC did not reach the merits; it suspended the lower judgment indefinitely, dismissed the appeal under BCO 42-7, rebuked Pacific Presbytery, and urged greater care in preserving, transcribing, and transmitting testimony. Dismissal therefore did not leave the challenged judgment enforceable. A separate concurrence suggested recording testimony or hiring a court reporter and questioned imprudent prosecutions.

The SJC sustained her complaint: she had submitted to regular trial, making her appeal in order under BCO 42-2, and her complaint was timely after Presbytery's advice caused the appeal to be renamed. It remanded for Presbytery to adjudicate the appeal. Filing the appeal suspended the Lord's Table censure pending final adjudication; the SJC questioned the contumacy ruling.

synopsis: A member suspended from the Lord's Table appealed after Presbytery let the Session resume her trial and failed to lift all suspensions. The SJC sustained the appeal, finding the Session's premature censure, truncated trial, and prosecutor-judge conflict manifested prejudice and made a fair trial impossible. It set aside all judgments and censures, treated the November 13, 2003 communion letter as non-censuring advice, and did not remand.

title: Paul W. Lee v. Korean Southwest
synopsis: A minister appealed three convictions and suspension that would automatically become indefinite absent repentance. The SJC sustained the appeal: unauthorized committee citations and admonition without process could not support guilt, and multiple trial violations were fatally prejudicial. It set aside the judgment, dismissed the citation and admonition charges, and revoked both censures. The inappropriate-language charge was not adjudicated on its merits; Presbytery could retry it on remand or dismiss it.

title: Chastain v. Heritage Presbytery
synopsis: An appeal challenged a presbytery's conviction of a minister for divisive behavior and its indefinite suspension from office and the sacraments. The SJC affirmed: the charge was lawful because publicly publishing disagreement with the session after it acted violated his ordination vows to subjection and peace/unity, even though “divisive” is not a constitutional term; the censure was not unjust absent repentance; procedural errors did not require reversal or remand. A dissent argued the charge failed BCO 29-1’s Scripture-proof requirement.

It did not sustain the threat conviction because the attorney’s letter was absent from the record. A dissent disputed the contumacy ruling.

Here the members had sought the Session’s advice, Presbytery had found no strong presumption of chargeable offenses, and renewed circulation would disturb the church’s peace; under those circumstances, the Session acted within its authority.

synopsis: TE James Bachmann appealed Nashville Presbytery's decision to replace his judicial commission's recommended admonition with indefinite suspension. The SJC sustained the appeal: Presbytery violated BCO 15-3 by dividing the verdict and amending the censure, which it had to approve or disapprove as a whole without debate. Bachmann's earlier procedural challenges were not sustained; his unconditional post-trial confession waived them. The SJC rendered the commission's judgment and admonition as its own decision, remanded to Presbytery, and restored Bachmann to good standing, subject to possible pastoral oversight items 2–4.

title: Frazier v. Nashville Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC denied a complaint challenging Nashville Presbytery's decision not to indict a teaching elder for allegedly sinful teaching on homosexuality and same-sex attraction. The adopted judgment held that the 147-page record showed Presbytery fulfilled its BCO 31-2 investigatory duty and did not show it erred in judgment when it declined process; the complaint was denied 20-0-1. Concurring opinions raised concerns about committee recusal, record clarity, and exegetical uses of Scripture, but they were separate and did not alter the denial.

title: Glen Mapes v. Metropolitan New York Presbytery
Sartorius v. Siouxlands Presbytery
synopsis: Did a presbytery fail in its duty to condemn erroneous opinions by acquitting a minister on theological-error charges? The SJC denied the complaint, leaving the acquittal undisturbed. A complaint against a not-guilty verdict cannot provoke a retrial at the superior court; under BCO 43 the superior court may only annul or remand, not reverse, and the complainant bore the burden to show error from the record. The record contained the defendant's testimony, including recantations or clarifications, Defense Exhibit 1, and witness testimony sufficient to refrain from contradicting the trial court. The SJC expressly did not decide the defendant's actual views. A separate concurrence elaborated deference standards but did not change the judgment.

title: Crouse v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery
synopsis: A serving deacon nominated for ruling elder complained that his session removed his nomination before BCO 24-1 instruction or examination. The SJC held the session erred by adding an unwritten pre-examination 'vetting' removal and that Northwest Georgia Presbytery erred in approving it: BCO 24-1's sequence—instruction and examination before the session determines eligibility—is mandatory. The ruling reserved the session's sound discretion and the treatment of frivolous or clearly disqualified nominees. The complaint was sustained and remanded for adjudication consistent with the decision.

Chavalas’s later resignation did not abandon the appeal because he had appealed beforehand after a regular trial; no rebuke was issued.

title: Ruff v. Nashville Presbytery
synopsis: Nashville Presbytery's BCO 31-2 investigation of reports against TE George Grant was inadequately documented and internally inconsistent, and the evidence before Presbytery raised a strong presumption of guilt, the SJC held. It sustained the complaint, ruling that pastoral reconciliation does not displace the duty to institute judicial process, and remanded for further proceedings; it did not adjudicate Grant guilty. A concurrence agreed only in remanding to supplement the record under BCO 42-5 & 7.

title: Latimer v. Chicago Metro Presbytery
synopsis: A presbytery deposed a minister for violating his seventh vow by pursuing an unbiblical divorce after he filed a civil petition. The SJC sustained the appeal in part: the presbytery clearly erred in finding sin in the filing, because the record did not conclusively show intent to divorce rather than protect his children, and the wife's counter-filing undermined the failure-to-withdraw inference. The SJC rejected prejudice, irregularity, and venue claims, voided the trial judgment, and noted that his expired prior suspension left him a presbytery member without call. Divorce precedents are fact-specific.

synopsis: G. Rick Marshall appealed Pacific Presbytery, which failed to transmit a material part of the Record of the Case, causing irremediable injury. The SJC did not reach the merits; it suspended the lower judgment indefinitely, dismissed the appeal under BCO 42-7, rebuked Pacific Presbytery, and urged greater care in preserving, transcribing, and transmitting testimony. Dismissal therefore did not leave the challenged judgment enforceable. A separate concurrence suggested recording testimony or hiring a court reporter and questioned imprudent prosecutions.

title: Huffman v. Tennessee Valley Presbytery

The SJC found it judicially out of order because the case began and was nearly completed when the former rule provided review by complaint, and retroactive application would be unfair. It remanded for Presbytery to adjudicate the filing as a complaint at its next stated meeting; denial or failure to act permits review by the SJC. No merits issue was decided.

title: Nickoley v. Rocky Mountain
synopsis: Rocky Mountain Presbytery cited Pastor Bruce Nickoley for contumacy during his trial, after he allegedly refused to tell his congregation to stop picketing, and immediately deposed him without a hearing. On appeal, the SJC sustained the appeal, holding the Presbytery misapplied BCO provisions on confession, citation, refusal to testify, and deposition; Nickoley neither confessed nor refused to appear. Although presbyteries have general authority to maintain order, serious charges require due process. The SJC remanded, recommending either a new process beginning with BCO §32-3 or revocation of the deposition and reinstatement.

synopsis: After a church member and deacon was excommunicated by his session, he appealed to Evangel Presbytery. Presbytery found the appeal in order and appointed a commission, but then rescinded that action and never adjudicated the appeal. The SJC held Presbytery erred by failing to notify the appellant of the appeal hearing and by failing to adjudicate an appeal properly before it. It remanded under BCO 42-9 for proper adjudication and made no ruling on the remaining session-related merits issues.

title: Nancy A. Conrad et al. v. Central Carolina Presbytery
synopsis: After a Session corrected an earlier unauthorized removal from its rolls, then formally voted to remove the same members, the members challenged Presbytery's denial of their complaint, arguing that the new removal defied the prior decision. The SJC upheld Presbytery's action. It concluded that the record showed no unconstitutional procedure or BCO violation and that it could consider only facts properly in the record, not material from earlier cases offered in oral argument. The ruling left the later membership removal undisturbed.

title: Nickoley v. Rocky Mountain
synopsis: Rocky Mountain Presbytery cited Pastor Bruce Nickoley for contumacy during his trial, after he allegedly refused to tell his congregation to stop picketing, and immediately deposed him without a hearing. On appeal, the SJC sustained the appeal, holding the Presbytery misapplied BCO provisions on confession, citation, refusal to testify, and deposition; Nickoley neither confessed nor refused to appear. Although presbyteries have general authority to maintain order, serious charges require due process. The SJC remanded, recommending either a new process beginning with BCO §32-3 or revocation of the deposition and reinstatement.

The SJC denied remand because Presbytery had effectively adjudicated the complaint; the separate objection to proceeding without Black was not first filed below and was administratively out of order. It upheld Presbytery’s ruling that not every non-Calendar-Day view constitutes an exception. Because the record did not identify the licentiate’s precise view, the decision did not determine its acceptability or whether it could be taught.

It reversed excommunication because the record did not show impenitence or contumacy, which could not be inferred from exercising the right to remain silent. synopsis: A member challenged Presbytery’s affirmance of his excommunication, contending that SJC Case 97-9 had reversed his four guilty verdicts and precluded increased censure. The SJC did not sustain either issue. Case 97-9 had reversed only the original censure, leaving guilt intact. Because the offender bore the burden of showing repentance, and Session’s contrary factual determination received great deference absent clear error, the later excommunication remained in effect.

title: Carolyn Goerig v. Pacific Northwest Presbytery
synopsis: A church member challenged Pacific Northwest Presbytery's denial of her complaint that Faith Presbyterian Church (Tacoma) Session had banned her from worship and sought to erase her membership retroactively under BCO 38-4. The SJC sustained the complaint. Because she never joined Covenant PCA, BCO 46-3 left her membership under Faith's Session; the Session's proposed retroactive erasure did not comply with BCO 38-4's pastoral-oversight steps. The Presbytery therefore erred and should have remanded the matter to the Session. No separate merits relief beyond that remand directive appears.

The SJC affirmed KEP's denial and the guilt findings, but reversed the increased censures. An appellate court may not increase a censure under BCO 42-9; the trial court retains discretion to remove or increase an indefinite suspension, though the appellate court may recommend a lesser censure. The original suspension remained.

The SJC sustained the complaint on the remand issue: rescission of the censure did not dispose of pending charges, so Presbytery had to rehear the complaint and require the Session either to institute proper process or dismiss them. It declined to determine guilt without a trial record and rejected the claim that the censure’s prescribed form willfully took the Lord’s name in vain.

synopsis: A minister appealed convictions and indefinite suspension arising from conflict over Presbytery's direction that he resign. The SJC upheld all three convictions, finding two procedural errors nonprejudicial and rejecting the other preserved challenges. But Presbytery could not treat its authority to dissolve a pastoral relationship as authority to compel resignation on pain of discipline. The SJC therefore vacated the censure and dissolution of the call and remanded for reconsideration of censure; Grady's separate administrative suspension remained effective.

Bachmann's earlier procedural challenges were not sustained; his unconditional post-trial confession waived them. The SJC rendered the commission's judgment and admonition as its own decision, remanded to Presbytery, and restored Bachmann to good standing, subject to possible pastoral oversight items 2–4.

The SJC partially sustained the complaint: prior indefinite suspension was not constitutionally required, but Presbytery properly found excommunication too severe because the trial record contained no evidence of contumacy. synopsis: At issue was whether North Texas Presbytery wrongly denied a complaint challenging Fort Worth Presbyterian Church’s “Special Case Felons” integration policy as contrary to Scripture. It did not decide whether the excommunication was proper; that issue remained for Presbytery to hear.

topics: in the space of six days

synopsis: Mt. Carmel Session challenged New Jersey Presbytery's creation-days resolution, arguing that the Westminster Standards require six consecutive twenty-four-hour days. The SJC majority concluded that Presbytery could resolve the doctrinal question under BCO 11-4 and that prior Assembly actions permitted latitude on the length of the creation days. The General Assembly rejected the minority report, adopted the majority report, and denied the complaint.

title: Nancy A. Conrad et al. v. Central Carolina Presbytery
synopsis: After a Session corrected an earlier unauthorized removal from its rolls, then formally voted to remove the same members, the members challenged Presbytery's denial of their complaint, arguing that the new removal defied the prior decision. The SJC upheld Presbytery's action. It concluded that the record showed no unconstitutional procedure or BCO violation and that it could consider only facts properly in the record, not material from earlier cases offered in oral argument. The ruling left the later membership removal undisturbed.

title: Nickoley v. Rocky Mountain
synopsis: Rocky Mountain Presbytery cited Pastor Bruce Nickoley for contumacy during his trial, after he allegedly refused to tell his congregation to stop picketing, and immediately deposed him without a hearing. On appeal, the SJC sustained the appeal, holding the Presbytery misapplied BCO provisions on confession, citation, refusal to testify, and deposition; Nickoley neither confessed nor refused to appear. Although presbyteries have general authority to maintain order, serious charges require due process. The SJC remanded, recommending either a new process beginning with BCO §32-3 or revocation of the deposition and reinstatement.

title: St. Paul Session, et al. v. Central Florida Presbytery
synopsis: The St. Paul Session and other Central Florida presbyters complained that Presbytery wrongly sustained a commission report denying the Session complaint and declining to find a strong presumption of guilt against Pastor John Hutchinson. The SJC denied the complaint on both issues. It held CFP permissibly directed a BCO 31-2 investigation and chose its own procedures; procedural irregularities and possible bias did not show BCO 39-3 clear error, though the panel criticized CFP’s handling. A lone dissent would remand, alleging the commission ignored the substance of 41 of 45 specifications.

Dallison complained that increasing the censure required fresh charges and trial. The SJC disagreed: his BCO 38-1 confession waived trial rights as to the original charge; the offender then had to satisfy the court of repentance, and the presbytery could investigate and impose higher censure under BCO 37-3, 37-4, 37-8, and 34-4b. The complaint was not sustained.

title: Christ Covenant Church Session v. Central Carolina Presbytery
synopsis: Christ Covenant Church Session complained under BCO 43 that Central Carolina Presbytery wrongly annulled the session trial commission's judgment and found due-process error concerning H. The SJC did not reach the merits. It held the case not judicially in order because H's complaint to the Session was untimely: it exceeded the thirty-day requirement of BCO 43-2 and came more than eighty days after the oral verdict. The ruling thus turned on a procedural gate, making no merits ruling on Presbytery's annulment or its due-process rationale.

synopsis: The SJC sustained a session's timely complaint that Louisiana Presbytery barred one of its members from the Lord's Table after assuming original jurisdiction. Under BCO 33-1, a presbytery may assume jurisdiction only when the session 'refuses to act'; because the session had investigated and found no strong presumption of guilt, it acted, so LAP never acquired jurisdiction. The censure was therefore a nullity, and the member remained under his session. The SJC also held the jurisdictional assumption reviewable despite no timely complaint against it. Three commissioners dissented.

Because Kim had not submitted to a regular trial, he was not entitled to appeal under BCO 42-2; the Presbytery had instead found him guilty of contumacy and deposed him from office under BCO 34-4. The ruling disposes of the appeal without reaching its merits and leaves the deposition in force.

synopsis: SJC sustained TE Philip Blevins's complaint against Westminster Presbytery, holding the Blevins/Seufert complaint was timely despite the commission's February 3, 2004 untimeliness ruling. The SJC did not decide the wife's divorce grounds or the Session's merits; it remanded for Presbytery to rehear the Session and Warhurst complaints with the Blevins/Seufert merits considered. A concurrence added that no full new trial is required.

synopsis: An appellant under suspension from the sacraments challenged the presbytery's judicial commission process and censure. Treated as a complaint, it was also out of order: it had not first been presented to the presbytery, and the 30-day period had expired. title: Ruff v. Nashville Presbytery
synopsis: Nashville Presbytery's BCO 31-2 investigation of reports against TE George Grant was inadequately documented and internally inconsistent, and the evidence before Presbytery raised a strong presumption of guilt, the SJC held. It sustained the complaint, ruling that pastoral reconciliation does not displace the duty to institute judicial process, and remanded for further proceedings; it did not adjudicate Grant guilty. A concurrence agreed only in remanding to supplement the record under BCO 42-5 & 7.

title: Lee v. Korean Eastern Presbytery
synopsis: Korean Eastern Presbytery dismissed TE Eliot Lee's charges against two teaching elders without trial, and the SJC sustained Lee's complaint that this was unconstitutional. Although a presbytery may dismiss charges under BCO 29-1, 32-20, 34-2, or 31-8, it bears the burden of documenting that basis; KEP did not. The SJC refused Lee's request that it enter the guilt verdicts the presbytery should have reached—that power exists on appeal, not complaint. It remanded for KEP to begin process under BCO 32.

Ruff challenged Presbytery's failure to investigate a teaching elder, but BCO 43 requires a complaint against an act or decision; lack of action qualifies only when a court meeting has occurred and the court failed to act. Presbytery's nearest antecedent meeting was August 18, 2010, and Ruff filed October 27, 2010, beyond BCO 43-2's thirty-day limit. Because the defect could not be cured, the case was dismissed without reaching the merits; a separate objection disputed that ruling.

No merits review appears; the adopted vote was 18 concurring, 2 not qualified, and 4 absent.

title: Hedman v. Pacific Northwest Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC denied RE Gerald Hedman's complaint against Pacific Northwest Presbytery, which had adopted five not-guilty judgments on charges that TE Peter Leithart's baptism, covenant, imputation, justification, and union-with-Christ views contradicted the Westminster Standards. Bound to the record and clear-error review, the SJC found no procedural violation and insufficient evidence that Presbytery clearly erred. It left the verdicts undisturbed, declined to endorse Leithart's views generally, and urged continued clarification of his non-standard terminology. A separate dissent would have found error and ordered a new trial or reference.

The adopted ruling gives no further rationale and carried 13 concurring, 5 dissenting, 1 abstaining, 1 disqualified, and 4 absent. A dissent argued the record did contain an adjudicable Session action and that the cited OMSJC provision did not list the ground used; a separate written objection challenged a panel member's participation.

title: Dunn and Pesnell v. Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery
synopsis: The complaint challenged Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery’s November 17, 2012 vote adopting its Complaint Commission’s recommendation to institute process and try TE David Swavely. The SJC did not sustain it. Although the record showed possible procedural irregularities—including unauthorized circulation of an earlier complaint—the SJC found no reversible error: presbyteries receive deference on factual records and broad latitude to judge the sufficiency of investigations. The recommendation to proceed to trial stands, subject to later parliamentary action. The SJC did not decide Swavely’s guilt.

synopsis: The SJC sustained the Session's complaint against Presbytery. Presbytery had ruled a member's original complaint administratively out of order as untimely but then remanded the matter to the Session; the SJC held that once out of order, no complaint remained to remand. It also held Presbytery could not direct or instruct the Session to initiate formal process without BCO 40-5's required citation step, so those directions were null and void. The member remained under the Session's jurisdiction; the civil trespass order was not ecclesiastical discipline and did not alter membership.

synopsis: Hahn challenged Presbytery’s ruling that CTKPC Session lawfully excluded him from that congregation’s worship until a psychiatric evaluation addressed safety concerns. The SJC denied the complaint. Applying BCO 39-3.3, it found no clear error in the lower courts’ credibility and discretionary judgments, given Session’s familiarity with the people and events. It characterized the restriction as informal pastoral safety guidance, not judicial discipline: it did not bar sacraments, worship elsewhere, or transfer, and attendance could resume upon medical assurance. The conditional local restriction therefore remained undisturbed.

The SJC found his complaint administratively out of order and dismissed it because he was not a commissioner at Presbytery’s January 2013 meeting; originating a BCO 40-5 report did not confer standing. Separately, the SJC accepted jurisdiction over Presbytery’s failure to respond and remitted the matter for constitutional disposition, without deciding whether the Session committed the alleged delinquencies.

Dismissal therefore did not leave the challenged judgment enforceable. A separate concurrence suggested recording testimony or hiring a court reporter and questioned imprudent prosecutions.

The ruling did not decide the indictment objection’s merits.

title: Thompson v. South Florida Presbytery
synopsis: After a Session excommunicated a member without trial for contumacy, the SJC sustained his complaint and annulled the contumacy judgment, excommunication, and later Session and Presbytery actions. No mutually agreed BCO 38-1 confession existed, and declining a confession meeting was not immediately censurable objective contumacy under BCO 32-6; subjective contumacy required confession or trial. He reverted to membership under pending indictment. The SJC did not find the indictment unconstitutional, decide trial guilt, or consider the unpleaded trespass warning.

The SJC dismissed. The November 10, 2015 challenge was untimely under BCO 43-2's 60-day filing rule; the February 9, 2016 challenge was not a proper complaint because it targeted committee activities, not a court's act or decision. synopsis: A complainant challenged Nashville Presbytery's handling of allegations against a teaching elder. The SJC held the matter judicially out of order and dismissed it, finding the original filing with the church session was not a BCO 43-1 complaint because the session lacked jurisdiction over the teaching elder. Presbytery properly treated the allegations as BCO 31-2/34-1 reports, and the complainant, not a Nashville member, lacked standing to complain about that new action. A nine-member dissent argued the filing of charges conferred standing under prior SJC cases.

title: Fordice v. Pacific Northwest Presbytery
synopsis: A church member challenged Presbytery’s denial of his complaint after it resolved accusations against a minister through a BCO 38-1 confession rather than trial. The SJC held that using confession without process was not itself error, but the statement and confession failed to correlate with and address the specific allegations. It sustained the complaint, annulled the denial, and remanded for Presbytery to amend the documents, institute process, reactivate the investigative committee, or otherwise respond directly and specifically to the unresolved allegations.

The complaint was dismissed without a merits ruling.

It also held that declaring the elder not in good standing removed rights without process, but left his properly imposed suspension effective. It rejected objections to discussion, questioning, and the timely submission charge, which could proceed without any determination of guilt.

title: Wills v. Metro Atlanta Presbytery
synopsis: Did a presbytery violate the BCO or clearly err by dissolving a congregation without its consent? The SJC said no and denied the complaint. On the constitutional issue, it held that BCO 13-9.f grants dissolution power and BCO 40-6 does not impose formal process for it. On the discretionary issue, it found no clear error in the record. The denial left dissolution in place and warned that such action still requires sufficient justification and prudent, reviewable procedure.

synopsis: The SJC denied a complaint challenging Nashville Presbytery's decision not to indict a teaching elder for allegedly sinful teaching on homosexuality and same-sex attraction. The adopted judgment held that the 147-page record showed Presbytery fulfilled its BCO 31-2 investigatory duty and did not show it erred in judgment when it declined process; the complaint was denied 20-0-1. Concurring opinions raised concerns about committee recusal, record clarity, and exegetical uses of Scripture, but they were separate and did not alter the denial.

title: Webster & Fowler v. Heritage Presbytery
topics: fundamentals of the system of doctrine
synopsis: Did Heritage Presbytery err by cautioning a session and requesting that it postpone a candidate's election or ordination while a complaint about his qualifications was pending? The SJC said no and denied the complaint. The motion was advice, not an act for or requirement imposed on the session; the session could disregard it, and BCO 43-2 does not bar presbyters from discussing matters related to a complaint not yet before them. The SJC left undecided whether such discussions would disqualify presbyters, since the Ullrey complaint never reached presbytery.

synopsis: A member removed from the rolls under BCO 38-4 challenged Presbytery's ruling that she lacked standing to complain because she was no longer a member. The SJC sustained the complaint: standing under BCO 43-1 cannot be defeated by the very removal challenged. Removal under BCO 38-4 is pastoral discipline, a disciplinary case, not a merely administrative act. The SJC remanded to Presbytery to consider the complaint and take the action it should have taken—remand to the Session. The merits of the removal were not decided.

title: DeJong v. Session of Village Seven Presbyterian Church
synopsis: A ruling elder challenged Session’s elder-term proposal and its creation of Judicial and Governance Commissions. The SJC denied the first two claims: the Constitution does not regulate elder terms, and the Judicial Commission’s assigned business was sufficiently defined. It sustained the Governance Commission claim because sweeping authority and reversed delegation allowed that body to function as Session itself, contrary to BCO 15-1. Session’s third motion was annulled, but Session remained free to adopt a narrower, constitutionally compliant plan.

synopsis: Members challenged a voting restriction imposed at a congregational meeting. The SJC dismissed the complaint as judicially out of order because BCO 43-1 permits complaints against acts or decisions of church courts, and a congregation is not such a court. It identified other possible routes through a report to Presbytery or review of church records. The adopted decision did not decide whether the voting restriction was constitutionally valid.

title: BCO 40-5 Matter re NW Georgia
synopsis: Presbytery approved calls and installed three associate pastors after a constitutionally deficient election. The SJC found egregious error, including slate voting, a standing rather than ballot vote, and failure to determine and record the number of voters present under the then-current rule. It nevertheless denied the requested annulment of the installations because PCA judicial proceedings supplied no precedent and the remedy's legitimacy was doubtful. The SJC stayed further proceedings and declared the report concluded.

title: Biese et al. v. Tennessee Valley Presbytery
synopsis: Biese and others complained that Tennessee Valley Presbytery erred by approving Redeemer Church session minutes without exception—minutes noting a youth Super Bowl party—and by denying their complaint seeking a Sabbath exception. The SJC denied the complaint: because Presbytery gave no reasons for its actions, the record was insufficient to find it erred in interpreting the Constitution. A concurrence said the denial did not decide the Sabbath merits; a dissent would have held the complaint judicially out of order for lack of SJC jurisdiction over presbytery record review.

synopsis: Arizona Presbytery divested a minister without censure for prolonged lack of call after he had joined an EPCEW congregation and notified Presbytery of his withdrawal. The SJC sustained his appeal and reversed the divestiture because BCO 38-3(a) had already ended Presbytery's jurisdiction while he was in good standing and under no investigation or charges. It directed Presbytery to record the irregular withdrawal, acknowledge his new membership, and remove him from its roll.

title: Hann v. Pee Dee Presbytery

The adopted ruling was approved 17-2; Maynard and Sartorius dissented without stated reasons, four were absent, and Ross recused.

synopsis: Elders challenged Presbytery’s authority and vague instruction for its Shepherding Committee to “follow up” with their Session. The SJC denied the constitutional challenge because the record reasonably supported concern for the church’s peace and spiritual welfare, but sustained the challenge to Presbytery’s lack of specific direction and poor communication. The decision distinguishes prohibited mandatory visitation without cause from a reasonably justified visit, while requiring clarity about its objectives. It did not decide the underlying doxology dispute or order further relief.

title: Psiaki v. Pacific Northwest Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC sustained Psiaki’s complaint and held that the CPC Session erred by ordaining and installing officers elected at a February 5, 2023 congregational meeting where the congregation’s bylaw excluded communing members under 18 from voting. Reading BCO 6-4, 25-1, and 25-7 together, the SJC ruled that all communing members are entitled to vote and that local bylaws cannot impose an age restriction; the “good and regular standing” language addresses censure, not age. The decision did not annul the completed ordination/installation, but required future elections and installations to comply with the Constitution.

synopsis: A pastor complained that Presbytery upheld his Session’s refusal to give him financial reports prepared for Session members, while also alleging record-transmission, circularization, factual, and constitutional errors. title: Lovelace v. Northeast Presbytery (Case #2)
topics: membership status during pendency of case
synopsis: A member challenged Presbytery’s refusal, after investigation, to try four elders on favoritism charges and its ruling that her related complaint was out of order because dissolution of her church ended her PCA membership. The SJC denied the first item because BCO 31-2 permits declining process when investigation raises no strong presumption of guilt. It sustained the second: jurisdiction properly invoked while a communicant member is not lost through a later status change. No remand was expressly ordered.

synopsis: Smith challenged Northeast Presbytery’s ruling that his complaint was untimely and unconstitutional after it dissolved Grace Church and indefinitely postponed a proposed Braintree mission. The SJC sustained the complaint and remanded it for Presbytery adjudication. The May action first revealed Presbytery’s view that former members were outside the PCA, so the June complaint was timely. BCO 11-4 neither barred nor itself required care; responsibility arose here from the April referral to Presbytery’s missions committee. Care need not take the form of a mission, and mere dissolution alone would not create that responsibility.

title: Curtis v. Eastern Carolina Presbytery
topics: exceptions to Westminster Confession of Faith
synopsis: Eastern Carolina Presbytery referred to the SJC both TE Byron Curtis's complaint against Presbytery's order barring him from teaching his exceptions and TE Jeff Black's already-sustained complaint on the same subject. Without reaching the merits, the SJC remanded to the Presbytery for adjudication at the next stated meeting, directing that Curtis's complaint be heard. It reasoned that judicial complaints in process cannot be referred for mere advice and that, despite uncertainty about what the Presbytery sought, the lower court should hear the case first. Five SJC members dissented; the merits remained open.

synopsis: Black challenged Presbytery’s handling of his complaint and its ruling that a licentiate’s non-24-hour creation-day view was not an exception to the Westminster Standards. The SJC denied remand because Presbytery had effectively adjudicated the complaint; the separate objection to proceeding without Black was not first filed below and was administratively out of order. It upheld Presbytery’s ruling that not every non-Calendar-Day view constitutes an exception. Because the record did not identify the licentiate’s precise view, the decision did not determine its acceptability or whether it could be taught.

synopsis: Christ Covenant Church Session complained under BCO 43 that Central Carolina Presbytery wrongly annulled the session trial commission's judgment and found due-process error concerning H. The SJC did not reach the merits. It held the case not judicially in order because H's complaint to the Session was untimely: it exceeded the thirty-day requirement of BCO 43-2 and came more than eighty days after the oral verdict. The ruling thus turned on a procedural gate, making no merits ruling on Presbytery's annulment or its due-process rationale.

The chairman of Presbytery's Judicial Business Committee advised her that her appeal was out of order; Presbytery later ruled her complaint untimely. The SJC sustained her complaint: she had submitted to regular trial, making her appeal in order under BCO 42-2, and her complaint was timely after Presbytery's advice caused the appeal to be renamed. It remanded for Presbytery to adjudicate the appeal. Filing the appeal suspended the Lord's Table censure pending final adjudication; the SJC questioned the contumacy ruling.

synopsis: The SJC sustained a session's timely complaint that Louisiana Presbytery barred one of its members from the Lord's Table after assuming original jurisdiction. Under BCO 33-1, a presbytery may assume jurisdiction only when the session 'refuses to act'; because the session had investigated and found no strong presumption of guilt, it acted, so LAP never acquired jurisdiction. The censure was therefore a nullity, and the member remained under his session. The SJC also held the jurisdictional assumption reviewable despite no timely complaint against it. Three commissioners dissented.

synopsis: The SJC found Case 2003-6 judicially out of order because the challenged Eastern Carolina Presbytery action was only advice in response to a BCO 41-1 reference from White Oak Session, not a binding or complainable doctrinal decision under BCO 41-3. The underlying dispute—whether elders could hold and teach a broader atonement view—was therefore not reached. The adopted vote was 17 concurring, 1 dissenting, with 1 abstention and 4 absent. The dissent argued Presbytery's 'not allowed' language read as compulsory final disposition.

title: Blevins v. Westminster
synopsis: SJC sustained TE Philip Blevins's complaint against Westminster Presbytery, holding the Blevins/Seufert complaint was timely despite the commission's February 3, 2004 untimeliness ruling. The wife's April 2003 letter was essentially a BCO 35-13 request to review new evidence, and the Session's May 2003 denial was a new complaintable decision. The SJC did not decide the wife's divorce grounds or the Session's merits; it remanded for Presbytery to rehear the Session and Warhurst complaints with the Blevins/Seufert merits considered. A concurrence added that no full new trial is required.

title: Nichols and Couch v. James River Presbytery
synopsis: Case 2002-03 was decided with Cases 2001-34 and 2002-02. The SJC ruled some constituent complaints out of order but sustained the central complaint that James River Presbytery unduly delayed acting on a congregation's proper request to dissolve its pastoral relationship; it denied a related complaint concerning a salary gift. The consolidated decision drew concurring and dissenting opinions.

The SJC sustained both issues: the petition should first have gone to the Session, and Presbytery and its Commission committed additional constitutional errors. Those errors did not excuse his refusal to obey Presbytery, however. Because he had been deposed in Case 2005-8, further action was moot; the SJC granted no remedy, vacatur, or remand.
